Statement on MeitY's notice to WhatsApp over the "usernames" feature

The Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology (MeitY) has sent WhatsApp a notice about the usernames feature it announced on 29 June 2026. The notice asks the company to explain, within three days, why regulatory action should not be taken against it "for launching a feature that may increase cybercrimes", and it directs the company "not to roll out this feature until the consultation on this point is achieved to the satisfaction of the Government". The Internet Freedom Foundation is concerned that the notice has no clear basis in law. It is an attempt by the executive to decide what a company may build and ship, which no statute permits.

The notice treats the launch of a lawful feature as a wrong the company must justify. That reverses the ordinary position especially given the absence of any clear legal power that exists. MeitY does not name any provision that lets it approve a product feature before release or order one withdrawn, because there is none, and the provisions it does cite do not supply that power.

Section 79 of the IT Act, 2000 is a safe harbour that protects an intermediary from liability for what its users post, so long as it observes due diligence. It decides when a platform can be held liable. It is not a power for MeitY to decide what features the platform may offer. Sections 66C and 66D punish identity theft and cheating by personation. They are criminal offences, tried by courts, aimed at the person who steals an identity, not at the maker of a tool that a third party misuses. Also, on MeitY's logic, a telecom operator could be told not to sell SIM cards because SIM cards are used in almost every online fraud. 

Rule 3(1)(b), Rule 3(2) and Rule 4 of the IT Rules, 2021 are due diligence and grievance obligations and cannot be converted into a licensing scheme. Section 69A, the one provision that lets MeitY control what appears online, permits the blocking of specific information through a set procedure. It says nothing about which features a company may build. Further the IT Rules, 2021 are subordinate legislation made under Sections 79 and 87 of the IT Act, and subordinate rules cannot travel beyond the parent statute (Ajoy Kumar Banerjee v. Union of India). If a rule cannot exceed the Act, a letter certainly cannot. The power to require prior permission for a feature is not in the Act, not in the Rules, and cannot be created by a notice. 

MeitY has tried this before. In March 2024 it told the same large intermediaries, among them AI Companies, to obtain its explicit permission before deploying under-tested AI models. That was criticised as an overreach that sought to build a licensing mechanism with no empowering provision in the IT Act, and within a fortnight MeitY withdrew it and dropped the permission requirement. This notice repeats the move for a single feature and goes further, because it names one company, sets a three-day clock, and bars the launch until MeitY is satisfied. 

This matters beyond WhatsApp. A power asserted against one company by letter can be turned on any company and any feature. On this reasoning MeitY could tell a browser not to switch on a privacy setting by default, or a payments app not to add a login method, each time until it was content. The notice also invokes traceability, through Rule 4(2) of the IT Rules, 2021 and the identification of the "first originator" of a message. Rule 4(2) has been challenged as exceeding its parent provision and resting on no law made by Parliament, and that challenge is pending before the Delhi High Court. Raising it against a feature meant to share fewer identifiers fits a pattern. 

We ask MeitY to state the exact provision of law under which this notice, and the direction to halt the roll-out, has been issued, and to withdraw that direction. It should stop using Section 79 and the contested traceability rule as leverage to control product design and to reverse features that improve privacy. Impersonation and fraud are real risks, but they are met by enforcing the criminal law against those who commit them, and by open processes that rest on identified legal powers. They are not met by MeitY deciding, in private and by letter, what features Indians may use. That is a licence raj for software features.

New Delhi, 1 July 2026

On October 3, BitChat co-founder Jack Dorsey shared an Apple App Review notice on X stating that the application had been removed from the India App Store following a blocking order issued by the Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology (MeitY) under Section 69A of the IT Act.

https://t.co/U7n9Gm93sQ

The blocking of social media accounts citing Section 79(3)(b) of the IT Act, 2000 is, in most if not all instances, being facilitated by the Sahyog Censorship Portal, first established through a MeitY Office Memorandum and subsequently formalised through amendments to the IT Rules, 2021 in Rule 3(1)(d). This portal is being provided by the Ministry of Home Affairs From our understanding and observed censorship trends, these Sahyog notices are being issued by at least 35 State Police Departments across the country who are, "nodal officers". See screenshot.

When a person's account is blocked, they typically receive inadequate information from the intermediary (Meta, Google, X), communications that merely cite Section 79(3)(b). X is not part of the Sahyog platform but is serviced through its own notification mechanism. Neither MeitY nor the police authority informs the user of the reasons for blocking, the date of the order, or the issuing authority. Hence, the first step for an affected party is therefore to write to MeitY and the intermediary requesting a copy of the order, since Rule 3(1)(d) of the IT Rules, 2021 imposes no confidentiality requirement. For the text of the rule, see screenshot.

Such requests are often refused, forcing affected users to approach a High Court first to obtain the order, and then, if it has been jurisdictionally issued in the same state where High Court proceedings are pending, to challenge it on merits. It is also unclear whether the review committees envisaged under Rule 3(1)(d) actually exist and their composition, contact details, and meeting dates are nowhere disclosed, leaving censored users without recourse.

This is a Kafkaesque system designed by MeitY and the MHA. It is the digital infrastructure of censorship under which users who criticise the government, comment on social and cultural issues, or opposition political parties are being silenced online. 

More information and analysis available here : https://t.co/XIVXL5WzI9

For any support or questions please always feel free email on legal@internetfreedom.in

Statement : The blocking of BitChat's code on GitHub is unconstitutional and authoritarian. 

New Delhi, 24 July 2026

The Internet Freedom Foundation (IFF) condemns the order issued by the Indian Cyber Crime Coordination Centre (I4C), Ministry of Home Affairs, directing GitHub to remove the code repositories of BitChat. 

The order, Notice No. 11072601011432, was issued at 11:16 pm on 23 July 2026 under Section 79(3)(b) of the Information Technology Act, 2000 read with Rule 3(1)(d) of the IT Rules, 2021. The order directs GitHub to disable access to three repositories, including the Android application and its release files, within three hours. It threatens the platform with loss of safe harbour and criminal prosecution. No copy was published by the Government of India. The public learnt of it from a post by @jack, whose team develops BitChat. Censorship in India now comes to light through disclosure by the censored.

Since 17 July 2026, the Ministry of Home Affairs has suspended mobile internet around Jantar Mantar as per public reports about five times, most recently within a 1.5 kilometre radius from 4 pm until midnight on 23 July. That radius takes in Janpath and parts of Connaught Place. Reports describe signal jammers at the protest site and people walking two kilometres before their phones work. Inside that zone a student separated from her group during a detention drive cannot send a message to say where she is. Thousands of students and young people have camped at Jantar Mantar since June, seeking accountability for examination irregularities. Permission for their march to Parliament was refused. Metro stations were shut and also internet connectivity has been blocked.

BitChat is an open source application built for exactly this situation. It passes messages from phone to phone over Bluetooth, without mobile networks or a central server. It is striking that the order does not identify a single unlawful message. It objects to what BitChat is. In its own words, the application is dangerous because it enables communication "even during network restrictions" and can "circumvent lawful restrictions" during "internet shutdowns". Hence, the government's objection is that citizens can speak to one another while it has switched the internet off. 

The order is illegal on at least four grounds. 

1. Section 79(3)(b) is not a blocking power. In Shreya Singhal v. Union of India (2015) 5 SCC 1, the Supreme Court read down the provision. Intermediaries may be required to act only on a court order, or a government notification confined to the grounds under Article 19(2) of the Constitution. Blocking is governed exclusively by Section 69A and the Blocking Rules, 2009, which require a hearing and reasons recorded in writing, subject to review. Directions issued under Section 79(3)(b), Rule 3(1)(d) and the Sahyog Portal evade these safeguards, and constitutional challenges to this parallel regime are pending before High Courts. 

2. The reasons in the order are circular. The order asserts that the repositories contain "information which is prohibited under any law" without naming any such information, and rests on what the application is "capable of" enabling. Anticipated misuse of a communications tool is not a lawful basis to prohibit the tool. By this logic a telephone exchange could be sealed. 

3. The order cites Section 43 of the IT Act, a civil compensation provision, alongside conspiracy and abetment offences under the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023, against a platform that hosts code. 

4. A three hour deadline issued close to midnight forecloses legal assessment and recourse, and fails the proportionality standard in Anuradha Bhasin v. Union of India (2020) 3 SCC 637.

The order also fails on its own terms as deleting a repository does not delete the application from any phone that carries it, and the mesh keeps functioning without servers. What the takedown actually prevents is scrutiny of the underlying code.

IFF demands that the Government of India:

1. Withdraw Notice No. 11072601011432 dated 23 July 2026 issued to GitHub.
2. Publish every takedown direction issued under Section 79(3)(b), Rule 3(1)(d) and the Sahyog Portal, with the reasons recorded for each.
3. Restore full connectivity around Jantar Mantar, publish all suspension orders, and disclose the legal authority for the deployment of jammers.

We stand with the developers and the young protesters whose speech this order seeks to silence.

🚨 BIG: Government of India has unveiled one of the most comprehensive legal frameworks to combat AI-generated deepfakes, synthetic media, misinformation and unlawful online content.

The framework brings together the IT Act, 2000, Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita (BNS), 2023, IT Rules, 2021, the 2026 IT Rules amendments, and the IndiaAI Governance Guidelines to strengthen digital safety and platform accountability.

Key highlights:

🔹 Mandatory AI Labelling: Platforms must clearly label AI-generated or synthetic content with traceable metadata so users can identify manipulated content and prevent deception.

🔹 Fastest Takedown Timelines Yet: Removal of unlawful content after a valid government or court notice has been reduced from 36 hours to just 3 hours. Grievance redressal timelines have also been tightened—from 72 hours to 36 hours, and 24 hours to 2 hours for sensitive content such as nudity, impersonation and similar categories.

🔹 IT Act, 2000: Covers penalties for computer-related offences, identity theft (Sec. 66C), online impersonation (66D), privacy violations (66E), publishing obscene or sexually explicit content (Secs. 67 & 67A), empowers blocking of unlawful content under Sec. 69A, removal directions under Sec. 79, and enables police investigation under Secs. 78 & 80.

🔹 Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023: Covers cheating by personation (Sec. 319), forgery through false electronic records (Sec. 336), spreading false reports or misinformation causing public mischief (Sec. 353), and organised cybercrime involving deepfake content (Sec. 111).

🔹 Strict Platform Obligations: Intermediaries must not host or share content that infringes rights, invades privacy, promotes hate or violence, harms children, violates intellectual property, misleads users about message origin, knowingly spreads false information, impersonates individuals (including using AI), threatens India's sovereignty, security or public order, or violates any applicable law.

🔹 Greater Accountability for Social Media Platforms: Significant Social Media Intermediaries (SSMIs) must assist law enforcement in tracing originators of serious content, deploy automated tools to detect unlawful content, publish compliance reports, appoint grievance and compliance officers, maintain India-based compliance infrastructure, and provide user verification, appeals and fair hearing mechanisms.

🔹 Zero Tolerance for Harmful AI: Platforms are now explicitly required to prevent AI-generated child sexual abuse material, non-consensual intimate imagery, deepfakes, AI impersonation, harmful synthetic media and other unlawful AI-generated content using reasonable technical measures and automated detection systems.

🔹 Legal Consequences: Failure to comply with the IT Rules can result in intermediaries losing their Section 79 safe-harbour protection, exposing them to prosecution and legal action under applicable laws.

🔹 Robust Enforcement Ecosystem: The framework will be enforced through Grievance Appellate Committees (GACs), the Indian Cyber Crime Coordination Centre (I4C), the SAHYOG Portal, the National Cyber Crime Reporting Portal, and law enforcement agencies. Citizens can report cybercrime and deepfakes through the National Cyber Crime Reporting Portal, with Helpline 1930 available for cyber fraud complaints.

🔹 Responsible AI Development: Under the IndiaAI Mission, the government is funding indigenous AI safety projects, including Saakshya (IIT Jodhpur & IIT Madras), AI Vishleshak, and IIT Kharagpur's Real-Time Voice Deepfake Detection System, alongside the India AI Governance Guidelines to promote safe, trusted and responsible AI deployment.

The message is clear: AI innovation is welcome, but deepfakes, impersonation, misinformation, child exploitation, and unlawful synthetic content will face significantly stricter regulation, faster takedowns, and stronger legal consequences than ever before.

The strategy works like this. You pick a starting point on the chart, for example the last major low. From there the indicator draws a line with the average price every buyer has paid since, weighted by volume. While Bitcoin closes above the line you hold it, and when it closes below you sell.
On a chart this often looks convincing. Price drops, touches the line and turns, two or three times. Before you trust it, one question matters: is the line there because the market respects it, or because you put it there?

—
𝗧𝗵𝗲 𝗽𝗿𝗼𝗺𝗶𝘀𝗲

Brian Shannon made the tool popular with his 2023 book "Maximum Trading Gains With Anchored VWAP". On 8 May 2026 the TradingView author AstralVision published a Bitcoin indicator that calls anchored VWAPs "among the most reliable dynamic support and resistance levels available".
At first sight Bitcoin agrees. Anchored at the last confirmed turning point, a high or low that stands out over 40 days on each side, the rule returned 44.8 percent a year after fees from July 2020 to October 2026. Holding returned 42.7 percent. The worst drawdown was minus 61.0 percent instead of minus 76.6 percent, and the rule passes the out-of-sample test of the Backtesting Arena validation tool.
𝗜𝗳 𝘁𝗵𝗲 𝘀𝘁𝗼𝗿𝘆 𝗲𝗻𝗱𝗲𝗱 𝗵𝗲𝗿𝗲, 𝘁𝗵𝗲 𝗶𝗻𝗱𝗶𝗰𝗮𝘁𝗼𝗿 𝘄𝗼𝘂𝗹𝗱 𝗵𝗮𝘃𝗲 𝗲𝗮𝗿𝗻𝗲𝗱 𝗶𝘁𝘀 𝗿𝗲𝗽𝘂𝘁𝗮𝘁𝗶𝗼𝗻.
One number is missing, though: what would have happened with the anchor somewhere else?

—
𝗧𝗵𝗲 𝘁𝗲𝘀𝘁

The anchor is the one thing you decide, so that is what the test changes. Five common anchor rules each ran against 1,000 copies. Every copy re-anchors at the same moments as the original, but at a random point within the previous 252 trading days. Everything else stays identical.
If the anchor carries information, the original has to beat most of its random copies. Here is the share of random anchors that did better:
Lowest low of the last 252 days: 99 percent.
Highest high of the last 252 days: 98 percent.
Last turning point, confirmed over 10, 20 or 40 days: 87, 62 and 39 percent.
None of the five places the line better than chance. The rule makes money because Bitcoin rose, and a rule that is long above a line stays long most of the time wherever the line sits. With a different anchor, the same rule lands anywhere between 17 and 79 percent a year.
𝗧𝗵𝗲 𝗮𝗻𝗰𝗵𝗼𝗿 𝗶𝘀 𝗮 𝗰𝗵𝗼𝗶𝗰𝗲, 𝗻𝗼𝘁 𝗶𝗻𝗳𝗼𝗿𝗺𝗮𝘁𝗶𝗼𝗻.

—
𝗧𝗵𝗲 𝘆𝗲𝗮𝗿𝗹𝘆 𝗹𝗼𝘄

The worst anchor is the one that sounds smartest. A line that starts at the 52-week low shows the entry price of everyone who bought the bottom, and that is exactly why it sits below price almost all the time. The rule was long on 79 percent of days.
In spring 2021 Bitcoin fell 45 percent from its April high. The rule stayed long the whole way and only sold on 23 May at $34,655. In 2022 every new low reset the anchor, every small rebound became a buy signal, and of 25 trades, 22 lost money. From April 2021 to January 2023 the drawdown reached minus 78.9 percent, deeper than simply holding.
𝗔 𝗹𝗶𝗻𝗲 𝘁𝗵𝗮𝘁 𝗮𝗹𝘄𝗮𝘆𝘀 𝘀𝗶𝘁𝘀 𝗯𝗲𝗹𝗼𝘄 𝗽𝗿𝗶𝗰𝗲 𝗰𝗮𝗻𝗻𝗼𝘁 𝘄𝗮𝗿𝗻 𝘆𝗼𝘂 𝗮𝗯𝗼𝘂𝘁 𝗮 𝗰𝗿𝗮𝘀𝗵.

—
𝗧𝗵𝗲 𝗼𝗯𝗷𝗲𝗰𝘁𝗶𝗼𝗻

"The volume is what makes it work. It is the V in the name."
The same five rules also ran with a plain average of prices since the anchor, no volume weighting. Volume helped in two cases and hurt in three, and using the close instead of the average of high, low and close flips two of the signs. There is no consistent direction.
𝗩𝗼𝗹𝘂𝗺𝗲 𝗶𝘀 𝗻𝗲𝗶𝘁𝗵𝗲𝗿 𝘁𝗵𝗲 𝗽𝗿𝗼𝗯𝗹𝗲𝗺 𝗻𝗼𝗿 𝘁𝗵𝗲 𝗳𝗶𝘅; 𝘁𝗵𝗲 𝗮𝗻𝗰𝗵𝗼𝗿 𝗶𝘀 𝘁𝗵𝗲 𝗽𝗿𝗼𝗯𝗹𝗲𝗺.

—
𝗪𝗵𝗮𝘁 𝘁𝗼 𝗱𝗼 𝗶𝗻𝘀𝘁𝗲𝗮𝗱

A bounce off an anchored VWAP shows which anchor someone picked, not that the market defends the line. If you use one, test your own anchor rule against random anchors first. If it does not beat more than 95 percent of them, it carries no information.
If all you want is a trend filter, the 200-day line has no starting point to choose. Long above it and cash below returned 41.8 percent a year over the same period, with a worst drawdown of minus 63.4 percent.
𝗜𝗳 𝘆𝗼𝘂 𝗰𝗵𝗼𝗼𝘀𝗲 𝘄𝗵𝗲𝗿𝗲 𝘁𝗵𝗲 𝗹𝗶𝗻𝗲 𝘀𝘁𝗮𝗿𝘁𝘀, 𝗮 𝗰𝗵𝗮𝗿𝘁 𝗰𝗮𝗻𝗻𝗼𝘁 𝘁𝗲𝗹𝗹 𝘆𝗼𝘂 𝘄𝗵𝗲𝘁𝗵𝗲𝗿 𝗶𝘁 𝗺𝗮𝘁𝘁𝗲𝗿𝘀.
The test covers Bitcoin on daily candles only. The open question is whether any market has an anchor rule that beats 95 percent of its random copies.

Karnataka Police Chief Issues Strict Guidelines on Non‑Consensual Image Sharing: “Consent to Film Is Not Consent to Share”

Bengaluru

In a decisive move to combat digital harassment and safeguard victims’ rights, Karnataka’s DG & IGP Dr M. A.Saleem has issued an order mandating immediate registration of FIRs in cases involving the non‑consensual sharing of intimate images and videos.

The directive clarifies that consent to be photographed or filmed does not extend to dissemination.“There is a difference between consent to capture and consent to dissemination,” the order states, underscoring that unauthorized sharing violates the fundamental Right to Privacy under Article 21 of the Constitution.

The guidelines follow reports of police stations refusing or delaying complaints on the grounds of prior consent. To end such practices, officers have been warned of strict disciplinary action if they fail to register FIRs in cases of “revenge pornography,” “blackmail videos,” or “sextortion.”

Relevant laws must be applied, including Section 77 of the BNS, 2023 and Sections 66(E), 67 and 67(A) of the IT Act, 2000. In sextortion cases, charges of extortion and criminal intimidation under the BNS must also be invoked.Officers are instructed to register Zero FIRs under the BNSS, 2023 if the offense occurs outside their jurisdiction and transfer them promptly.

Victim protection has been prioritized, with strict confidentiality of identities and sensitive handling of complainants. Wherever possible, female victims’ statements must be recorded by female officers. Investigating officers are also directed to issue rapid takedown notices to platforms under the IT Act and IT Rules, 2021, while ensuring preservation of digital evidence.

The order further calls for close coordination between local police, Cyber Police Stations and the CID Cyber Division to track accounts, conduct technical investigations, and analyze forensic evidence.

text:
The draft "IT Rules 2026" (Second Amendment to 2021 rules, proposed March 30 by MeitY, comments open till Apr 14) makes govt advisories binding on platforms like X/Instagram. Non-compliance risks losing safe harbor protection (no liability shield for user content).

It also extends blocking/grievance rules to news/current affairs posted by individual users/creators (not just registered publishers), treating more content like publisher material.

Govt goal: curb fake news, hate, misinformation faster. Critics say it overreaches on free speech & targets independent voices.

Not inherently "wrong"—it's a policy trade-off for accountability vs openness. Implementation will decide if it balances or chills expression. Specific part bugging you?

text:
Hi Creators!

ASK ME QUESTIONS REGARDING X RULES ON POSTING YOUR CONTENT.

I WILL ANSWER THEN WITH PLEASURE.

Here’s one hypothetical question that intrigues every creator’s mind.

And the answer follows.

Q: Does X take it as violation of rules if posts created by AI or Grok are posted on the platform?

A: No. Posting content created by AI, including Grok, is not itself a violation of X’s rules.

X’s rules focus on deception, harm, spam, and certain restricted categories—not on whether a person or a model wrote or generated the post.

What the rules actually say:

Under the Authenticity policy, synthetic or manipulated media is restricted only when it is shared deceptively and is likely to cause harm (for example, widespread confusion on public issues, public-safety risk, or serious harm). 

That includes media of a real person fabricated or simulated with AI. Sharing the same kind of media in a non-deceptive way is allowed. X may also label synthetic media so people can see the context.
Ordinary AI-written text, images, or video—jokes, commentary, art, summaries, fictional scenes, and similar posts—does not violate the rules just because AI made them.

Narrower limits that do apply: 

•Creator Revenue Sharing (announced March 2026): unlabeled AI-generated videos of armed conflict can get a creator suspended from the revenue program for 90 days, and permanently on a repeat. That is a monetization penalty, not a general ban on AI posts.

•Spam and platform manipulation still apply. Bulk, duplicative, or automated posting that manipulates reach or trends can be enforced whether a human or an AI wrote it. Developer rules also require prior approval for AI-powered automated reply bots.

•Fake personas that use AI-generated profile photos or bios to deceive others are not allowed.

•AI-generated child sexual exploitation material is prohibited, as is non-consensual intimate imagery (including synthetic). Consensual adult AI content is allowed if it is labeled like other adult content.

•In India, under the IT Rules Amendment 2026, users must declare synthetically generated information that looks real and label it prominently. X says it watermarks images and videos generated or edited by Grok.

So a normal post drafted or illustrated by Grok is fine. Problems arise only if the post is spam, impersonation, unlabeled misleading media that can cause harm, or another existing rule violation.

The new Indian IT Rules 2026 (Amendment) mandate labeling for AI-generated content (SGI: synthetic audio/visuals appearing real). Key points:

- Users declare AI use; platforms verify & add prominent labels + metadata for traceability.
- No unlabeled AI content allowed.
- Takedowns: 2-3 hours for deepfakes/objectionable material (down from 24-36h).
- Effective Feb 20, 2026.
- Non-compliance risks penalties under IT Act, loss of safe harbor for platforms.

How to access Polymarket in India without a VPN.

Indian ISPs (Jio, Airtel, Vi, BSNL) have blocked @Polymarket at the DNS level.

Steps to fix it ⬇️

━━━━━━━━━━━━━
ANDROID

1. Settings → Network & Internet (or Connections)
2. Tap Private DNS
3. Select "Private DNS provider hostname"
4. Enter: https://t.co/vGTkSv7Un9
5. Save

Alternative hostname: https://t.co/uozbWpgpS7

Works on both Wi-Fi AND mobile data. Encrypted by default. Easiest method of all.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━
iPHONE / iPAD

Wi-Fi only (iOS limitation):
1. Settings → Wi-Fi → tap (i) next to your network
2. Configure DNS → Manual
3. Remove existing entries
4. Add 1.1.1.1 and 1.0.0.1
5. Save

For mobile data: install the "1.1.1.1: Faster Internet" app by Cloudflare from App Store. It sets up a system-wide profile.

The app uses iOS's VPN framework but is NOT a real VPN. It doesn't hide your IP or change location. It just reroutes DNS queries system-wide. Free, no signup, made by Cloudflare.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━
WINDOWS 11 / 10

1. Settings → Network & Internet → Wi-Fi (or Ethernet)
2. Click your active connection
3. Scroll to "DNS server assignment" → Edit
4. Change to Manual → toggle IPv4 on
5. Preferred: 1.1.1.1 | Alternate: 1.0.0.1
6. Save

Press Windows key → type "cmd" → right-click "Command Prompt" → Run as administrator → Yes. Black window opens. Type ipconfig /flushdns, press Enter.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━
macOS

1. System Settings → Network
2. Click your active connection → Details
3. Click DNS in sidebar
4. Click + and add 1.1.1.1, then 1.0.0.1
5. Remove existing ISP entries (select, click −)
6. OK → Apply

Open Terminal: press Cmd + Space → type "Terminal" → Enter. Copy-paste sudo dscacheutil -flushcache; sudo killall -HUP mDNSResponder, press Enter, type your Mac password (invisible while typing, that's normal), press Enter.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━
ROUTER (covers every device on Wi-Fi)

1. Open 192.168.1.1 or 192.168.0.1 in browser
2. Login (credentials usually on router sticker)
3. Find DNS settings (under WAN, Internet, or DHCP)
4. Primary: 1.1.1.1 | Secondary: 1.0.0.1
5. Save and reboot router

Best option if you want laptop + phone + smart TV + everything to work without per-device setup.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━
VERIFY IT WORKED

Open browser: visit https://1.1.1.1/help

It'll confirm you're using Cloudflare DNS + whether DNS-over-HTTPS is active. Then try polymarket(dot)com

━━━━━━━━━━━━━
IF DNS ALONE DOESN'T WORK

Some ISPs use Deep Packet Inspection (DPI) or SNI-based blocking. In that case:

• Use Firefox or Brave → enable DNS-over-HTTPS in settings (encrypts the DNS query so ISP can't see it)

• Android Private DNS method above already does this by default

*STATEMENT: Escalating Digital Censorship in India*

*New Delhi, February 28, 2026*

The Internet Freedom Foundation (IFF) is concerned by a cluster of online blocking and takedown actions and ISP level service disruptions reported between 24–28 February 2026. Across these incidents, users and affected services face restrictions without clear, timely reasons and without access to the underlying orders needed to challenge state action by exercising their rights to obtain legal remedy.

Developers reported severe, uneven disruption in access to Supabase across multiple Indian networks. Reporting indicates the disruption followed a government direction, with accounts suggesting use of Section 69A of the Information Technology Act, 2000. Yet there has been no public statement of the grounds, scope, or duration, and no accessible order for those impacted. Supabase has publicly stated that its domains became inaccessible due to a “ministry order”, and users have been pushed to workarounds such as alternative DNS or VPNs. In parallel, users on X (formerly Twitter) continue to receive “withheld in India” notices restricting specific posts within the country. Such notices usually do not provide the government order or its reasoning. Hence, for those who are being censored the basics of natural justice of a notice, opportunity for a hearing and remedy are delayed or absent.

This is enabled by secrecy built into the blocking framework. Section 69A is implemented through the 2009 Blocking Rules, which contemplate a committee process and, where feasible, notice to intermediaries and identifiable originators. But they also impose “strict confidentiality” over requests and actions taken. When orders and reasons are secret by default, affected persons cannot test legality, necessity, proportionality, or factual errors except through protracted litigation. When in _Shreya Singhal v. Union of India_ (2015), the Supreme Court upheld Section 69A while relying on the existence of procedural safeguards and reasoned decisions, indicating that impacted users could approach court in writ remedies. However, due to the operational secrecy and providing copies of orders and notices those who are censored and prevented from obtaining judicial remedy.

The February 2026 amendments to the IT Rules, 2021 further increase these risks. The substituted Rule 3(1)(d) requires intermediaries to remove or disable access within three hours of receiving “actual knowledge”, which can arise from a court order or a written “reasoned intimation” by authorised government officers. While the rule lists what a “reasoned intimation” should contain, the legal basis, statutory provision, nature of the unlawful act, and specific URL/identifier, the three-hour window pressures platforms to comply promptly which may often occur without any substantive assessment. These inherently opaque censorship practices are being accelerated through "Sahyog" portal. Developed by the Indian Cybercrime Coordination Centre (I4C), the Sahyog portal operates entirely without statutory footing, only being anchored in the IT Rules, 2021 that are created by executive notification. It functions as a censorship clearinghouse that deliberately bypasses the established, albeit weak, procedural safeguards of Section 69A. By routing automated takedown directives directly to intermediaries under Section 79(3)(b) of the IT Act, the portal structurally excludes citizens and impacted users from the grievance process.

We demand that the government introduce strictly judicially enforceable transparency requirements, publish all blocking orders, and restore the principles of natural justice to India's platform governance framework. Based on requests from our community we will also next week launch a rough public sheet in which social media users can input and add information on digital censorship.

Starlink’s low-Earth orbit (LEO) satellite architecture introduces unique challenges to national security, regulatory enforcement, and sovereignty. Unlike terrestrial telecom networks that rely entirely on local cell towers and fiber routes under domestic jurisdiction, satellite internet fundamentally shifts control over communications infrastructure.

### 1. Bypassing Lawful Interception and Surveillance

* **Absence of Local Gateways:** Indian telecom regulations (under the Global Mobile Personal Communications by Satellite, or GMPCS, framework) mandate that all voice and data traffic originating in India must route through physically inspected ground earth stations/gateways located within the country. Starlink uses **Inter-Satellite Links (ISL / laser mesh)** and direct-to-device routing, meaning user traffic can potentially hop between satellites and downlink at a ground station outside Indian territory, entirely bypassing Indian intelligence agencies.
* **End-to-End Encryption:** Without direct physical gateway taps, domestic security services cannot carry out court-approved, lawful interception of voice-over-IP (VoIP) or data streams used by hostile actors.

### 2. Operational Use by Insurgents and Cross-Border Militants

* **Field Portability:** Starlink user terminals (dish antennas) are compact, low-power, and easily run off portable battery banks or small generators.
* **Smuggling and Shadow Usage:** In contested border zones, conflict corridors, or remote regions (such as Jammu & Kashmir, the Northeast, or coastal outposts), smuggled terminals could give insurgent or terrorist groups resilient, untraceable communication channels.
* **Resistance to Conventional Electronic Warfare:** Starlink utilizes narrow, electronically steered phased-array beams that rapidly hop between moving LEO satellites, making them substantially more resistant to conventional terrestrial jamming than legacy geostationary (GEO) satellite links.

### 3. Circumvention of State Internet Shutdowns

* **Loss of Crisis Management Controls:** Under Section 5(2) of the Indian Telegraph Act / Telecommunications Act, state administrations frequently order localized internet blackouts during severe civil unrest, communal violence, or anti-terror operations to prevent coordinated mobilization.
* **Leaked Coverage & Imperfect Geofencing:** Because satellite footprints do not align cleanly with geographic borders, or because geofencing restrictions can be modified remotely or bypassed, foreign satellite internet can maintain an active connection inside blackout zones.

### 4. Data Sovereignty and Foreign Intelligence Exposure

* **Jurisdiction Under the US CLOUD Act:** SpaceX is a US-incorporated entity. Under US legal frameworks (such as the CLOUD Act and FISA 702), US intelligence and law enforcement agencies can compel US tech companies to hand over stored user data, traffic metadata, or routing logs without notifying foreign governments.
* **Telemetry and Geolocation Signals:** Starlink terminals constantly transmit precise GPS and phased-array telemetry to coordinate beam pointing. A foreign private company possesses real-time visibility into the exact geographic coordinates, density, and activity patterns of all active terminals—posing an operational security risk around sensitive Indian military installations.

### 5. Dependency on a Single Foreign Entity During Conflict

* **Private Geopolitical Leverage:** The precedent set in the Ukraine conflict demonstrated that SpaceX's executive leadership holds unilateral power over where satellite coverage is activated, throttled, or geofenced during military operations.
* **Strategic Autonomy Vulnerability:** If critical sectors, border posts, or remote administrative nodes become reliant on a foreign private network, India risks sudden operational denial or diplomatic leverage by a third party during a bilateral crisis or standoff.

### Mitigations Required by Indian Regulators

To address these security concerns, the Department of Telecommunications (DoT) and security agencies have held firm on strict compliance requirements before granting full commercial operational clearance:

* Mandatory installation of all routing **gateways on Indian soil**.
* Comprehensive **data localization**, ensuring Indian citizen metadata is not exported abroad.
* Seamless integration with Indian **lawful interception systems (LIM)**.
* Promotion of sovereign and allied alternatives (such as ISRO-supported infrastructure, OneWeb/Eutelsat, and Jio-SES) to avoid single-vendor dependency.

India is against one man holding the Kill-switch.

Then came Crimea.

Ukrainian sea drones reportedly lost connectivity during an operation.

In December 2024, Indian security forces reportedly recovered a Starlink terminal alongside weapons from a militant cache in Manipur.

Fine.

But that raises another question:

How are Starlink terminals reaching conflict zones and the hands of actors who should never have access to them?

🇮🇳 India isn't blocking Starlink

Let's get this straight.

Starlink isn't simply being “banned” by some anti-technology bureaucracy.

The company has already secured key regulatory approvals.

What remains involves spectrum allocation and security requirements.

That's not an oligarchic conspiracy.

That's a sovereign government asking a foreign satellite operator some very basic questions before allowing its network to operate across Indian territory.

🔐 Connectivity is infrastructure

A satellite network isn't just another consumer app.

It can become part of:

📡 Communications
🛰️ Critical infrastructure
🛡️ National security
🚨 Emergency response
⚔️ Military operations

And when the network is controlled by a private company headquartered outside India, questions about data, lawful access, network control, security auditing and continuity during a crisis aren't optional.

They're the whole point.

🎯 Strategic Lens

So yes, Elon.
Bring Starlink to India's villages.
Bring it to the mountains.
Bring it to the islands.
Bring connectivity to every Indian who needs it.
But do it on India's terms.

🇮🇳 Data stays under Indian jurisdiction.
🔐 Security audits happen under Indian rules.
⚖️ Indian law applies on Indian soil.
🛰️ And no switch in Texas decides what works over India during a national crisis.

That's not anti-progress.
That's sovereignty.

text:
DO NOT DO BUSINESS IN INDIA!

What exists is an Indian antitrust case in which the maximum penalty could be calculated on Apple’s global revenue, and Apple is fighting that formula in court.
India’s Competition Commission (CCI) has been investigating Apple’s App Store since 2021. Developers and groups including Match (Tinder), PhonePe and Paytm accused Apple of abusing a dominant position by forcing apps to use Apple’s in-app payment system and charging a commission of up to 30%. Apple denies the allegations. A final penalty order had still not been issued as of the latest reporting in September 2026; the Delhi High Court had barred the CCI from issuing one before 15 July 2026 while Apple’s challenge was pending.
The global-revenue issue comes from a 2023 amendment to the Competition Act and the CCI’s 2024 penalty guidelines. Those rules let the regulator fine a company up to 10% of its average global turnover from all products and services over the previous three financial years, not only India revenue or App Store revenue. Apple told the Delhi High Court that, applied to FY2022–FY2024, that cap would be about $38 billion. Its India revenue is far smaller — about $8.9 billion in FY25, against roughly $416 billion worldwide.
The CCI’s stated reason is deterrence. It argues that a fine based only on India sales would be too small to change the behavior of a global digital company, and that the global-turnover rule matches practice used in the EU. Apple calls the rule arbitrary, disproportionate and unconstitutional when the alleged conduct is limited to India, and has asked the court to strike it down. In May 2026 the CCI also shifted, at least for the investigation, to seeking Apple’s India-specific financials rather than global figures.

On the second day of January, in the great city of Granada, I saw the royal banners of Your Highnesses placed by force of arms on the towers of Alhambra, which is the fortress of the city. And I saw the Moorish king come to the city gates and kiss the royal hands of Your Highnesses, and those of the Prince, my Lord. Afterwards, in that same month, based on the information that I had given Your Highness about the land of India and about a Prince who is called the Great Khan, which in our language means 'King of Kings,' Your Highnesses decided to send me, Christopher Columbus, to the regions of India to see the Princes there and the peoples and the lands, and to learn of their disposition, and of everything, and the measures which could be taken for their conversion to our Holy Faith.

I informed Your Highnesses how this Great Khan and his predecessors had sent to Rome many times to beg for men learned in our Holy Faith so that his people might be instructed therein, and that the Holy Father has never furnished them, and therefore, many peoples believing in idolatries and receiving among themselves sects of perdition were lost. 

Your Highnesses, as Catholic Christians and Princes devoted to the Holy Christian faith and to the spreading of it, and as enemies of the Muslim sect and of all idolatries and heresies, ordered that I should go to the east, but not by land, as is customary. Further, my eldest son shall succeed to the same position, and so on from generation to generation for ever after. 

I left Granada on Saturday, the 12th day of the month of May in the same year of 1492 and went to the town of Palos, which is a seaport. I set my course for the Canary Islands of Your Highnesses, which are in the Ocean Sea, from there to embark on a voyage that will last until I arrive in the Indies and deliver the letter of Your Highnesses to those Princes, and do all that Your Highnesses have commanded me to do.

To this end I decided to write down everything I might do and see and experience on this voyage, from day to day, and very carefully. text:
Meta must stop silently withholding the Instagram accounts of independent journalists in India

13 October 2026

Since 9 October 2026, Instagram has made the accounts of several independent journalists covering the protests in Delhi unavailable in India. Utkarsh Gaur’s main account was withheld on 9 October, and Sunny Tomar’s soon after. On the night of 12 October, Instagram withheld the account of Shubhangi Das Gupta, a 22-year-old independent journalist, and her secondary account now appears to face the same action. Today, Journo Mirror’s account was withheld in India. Each received the same notice, that Instagram had, “temporarily restricted access to this account pursuant to legal requirements under India’s Information Technology (Intermediary Guidelines and Digital Media Ethics Code) Rules.” The notice does not say which authority made the demand, which rule was invoked, which post was objected to, or when the “temporary” restriction ends. It arrives as a no-reply notification after the account has gone dark, with no prior warning and no reason.

The same day, IANS and ANI, citing Delhi Police sources, reported that around 500 posts “spreading rumours or trying to create unrest among people” had been taken down. On 12 October, PTI had put the figure at 300, which means about 200 more in one day. The police have not said which posts were removed, from which platforms, under which provision, or whether anyone who posted them was told. We are also receiving reports of WhatsApp accounts being shut down and of mobile numbers being put through fresh KYC verification that leaves them unusable while it is pending. All of this comes alongside a timeline in which there was suspension of internet services and public transport in the heart of the national capital.

IFF condemns Meta’s withholding of entire journalist accounts on the strength of an unnamed “legal requirement”, and the Delhi Police’s practice of announcing a running censorship tally through anonymous sources. Meta must restore these accounts, tell every affected user who asked for the restriction and under what law, and stop turning demands about particular posts into the silencing of entire accounts.
The IT Rules, 2021, on which Meta’s notice relies, give it two routes to restrict content. The notice meets the conditions of neither. If Meta acted on a government demand, the route is Rule 3(1)(d). If Meta acted on its own, Rule 4(8) requires it, as a significant social media intermediary, to notify the user before disabling access, explain the grounds, and give an adequate opportunity to dispute the action. None of this happened. In this situation at present the entire burden will be shifted to the user to seek remedy under Rules 3(2) and 3A, where a user must first go to Meta’s Grievance Officer, who has 15 days, and then to the Grievance Appellate Committee, which has 30 more. In our experience these timelines are often not met, and a grievance against unnamed “legal requirements” is likely to be answered by pointing back to them. Whatever the intention, the effect is to keep a journalist off the platform for more than six weeks, exactly when her reporting matters most.

The Delhi Police figures raise their own questions. “Rumour” is not a ground for restricting speech under Article 19(2).  A count of 500 posts announced through unnamed sources does not let anyone tell whether a post was fabricated or simply showed something the police did not want seen. Nor is it obvious that 200 reasoned intimations, each signed by an officer of DIG rank and each identifying the provision, the unlawful act and the exact URL, were issued in a single day.

Our demands

1) Meta should restore every account withheld in connection with the protests where the underlying demand, if any, concerned specific posts, and restrict no more than the URLs named in a lawful reasoned intimation.
2) Meta should tell each affected user in writing which authority made the demand, the issuing officer’s rank, the provision relied on, the content identified, and when the restriction will end.
3) Meta should disclose whether its systems automatically extend demands about individual posts to entire accounts, and stop any such escalation immediately.
4) The Delhi Police should publish the takedown requests it has issued, with their number, platforms, provisions, issuing officers and reasons, as Anuradha Bhasin requires.
5) MeitY should ensure notice and a hearing to every person whose content is restricted, publish the outcome of the monthly Secretary-level review under Rule 3(1)(d), and stop using Section 79(3)(b), the Sahyog Portal and “temporary” restrictions under the IT Rules to bypass the safeguards of Section 69A.
If you have been affected

If your post or account was withheld or removed in connection with the protests, or you received a notice about a police data request, write to legal@internetfreedom.in for pro bono assistance. Keep screenshots of every notice, note the date and time, and delete nothing. Document, document, document.

text:
A Hyderabad founder spent four months building a B2B SaaS product. CRM integrations, three pricing tiers, onboarding that actually worked.

Two weeks before launch his co-founder asked what the cookie banner said.

There was no cookie banner. There were two documents, and neither of them had been written for this product.

The Terms of Service came from a competitor’s site. The Privacy Policy came from a template generator. Both had been pasted in during week one and never opened again.

He reached out to us with fourteen days on the clock. He was not asking for a document set. He wanted to know whether what he already had would survive contact with a paying customer.

So we read both documents against the product, not against each other.

The Privacy Policy said the platform collects name, email, and company name. That was true as far as it went.

It said nothing about the session replay tool running on every page, recording mouse movement and clicks from every visitor. 

Nothing about the analytics platform receiving behaviour data on export. 

Nothing about the CRM integration pulling contact records out of the customer’s own account.

Three tools were processing user data and a user reading the policy would never know they existed.

Under the DPDP Act, 2023 and the Rules notified on 13 November 2025, the notice has to itemize what is collected, the purpose, the retention, and who it is shared with. 

A policy that names three fields and omits three processors is not a short policy. It is an inaccurate one.

Then the liability cap. The template had a blank where the number goes and nobody had filled it in, so the contract capped his liability at zero.

Founders hear that and assume it is maximum protection. It is the opposite. 

A limitation clause that strips out all liability is the one most likely to be read against the drafter, and under UK law an unreasonable exclusion can be struck down entirely, which leaves the liability uncapped. 

The clause meant to protect him was the one most likely to disappear in a dispute.

The acceptable use clause prohibited uploading anything illegal. It said nothing about who owns uploaded data, whether the platform could use it to improve the product, or what happens to it when a subscription ends.

This is B2B. Every upload was a business customer’s data, which usually means it was someone else’s customer data two steps down the chain. Silence in the Terms is not a neutral position on that. If anything in the stack learns from customer data, silence means it is happening without a license.

The part I keep seeing is the sequence. 

Founders treat legal documents as a launch-day chore, something to generate the night before, when they are actually a product specification written in another language. 

The documents describe what the software does. If nobody checks them against what the software does, they describe a different product.

What I found harder to watch here was how well everything else had been built. 

Four months of careful work, and the one artefact he had outsourced to a template site was the first thing an enterprise buyer would open.

Here is what we did in the fourteen days.

We mapped every tool with access to user data, including the ones installed by his developer and never documented anywhere.

We rewrote the privacy notice to cover all of them, with purpose, retention, and third-party sharing set out against each.

We put a defensible number in the liability cap and rebuilt the clause around it.

We drafted the data ownership, permitted use, and model training position, plus deletion and export on termination.

We added the IT Rules disclosures, legal entity details and a named grievance officer, to the footer and the Terms.

The product launched three weeks later with a complete set. One week after that, the first enterprise prospect asked for a security and compliance review before signing. He had answers.

The comparison is not close. Two weeks of drafting before launch, against a DPDP penalty regime that runs up to ₹250 crore for security safeguard failures, and against the thing that actually kills early deals, which is a procurement team deciding you are too much work to onboard.

So here are three things to check before your next customer invite goes out.

Open your Privacy Policy and list every tool on your site that touches user data. Analytics, session replay, chat widget, CRM, email platform. If an SDK is installed and not named, your notice is wrong. Naming the obvious ones and skipping the rest is not a shorter policy.

Find the number in your liability cap. If the clause is blank, inherited, or set to zero, that is not conservative drafting. It is the clause your buyer’s counsel will spend the most time on.

Read what your Terms say about uploaded data. Ownership, permitted use, what happens on termination, and whether anything in your stack improves on it. If the document is silent on all four, you are relying on an assumption you never wrote down.

Two dates are now fixed. The Consent Manager framework switches on 13 November 2026. The obligations on notice, consent, security, and data principal rights apply from 13 May 2027.

Most founders who send us their documents believe the legal side is handled because the pages exist. 

The pages existing and the pages matching the product are different things, and the buyer’s counsel is the one who checks.

🚨 BREAKING: Government of India directs YouTube to take down Dhruv Rathee's (@dhruv_rathee) video titled "Can Hindus Eat Beef? | Kerala Story 2 Exposed."

The Grievance Appellate Committee (GAC), Ministry of Electronics & IT, by its Order dated 15 July 2026 (Appeal No. 8321/2026), has directed YouTube to remove the video within 24 hours of receiving the order.

Note: Although the order is dated 15.07.2026, it was uploaded publicly today (19 July 2026).

Key findings of the GAC:
• The video contains statements found to insult Bhagwan Shri Ram, Bhagwan Shri Krishna, and Sita Devi.
• It was found to make claims that they consumed meat and alcohol using disputed interpretations of scriptures.
• The GAC held that the content hurts the religious sentiments of crores of Hindus and is contrary to societal harmony.
• YouTube's free speech arguments were not accepted, with the order noting that freedom of expression is subject to the reasonable restrictions under Article 19(2) of the Constitution.

The order follows the Hon'ble Delhi High Court's direction dated 3 July 2026 requiring the appeal to be decided within 15 days.

The complainant has also stated that these findings may be relevant to a separate pending petition before a Magistrate seeking registration of an FIR against Dhruv Rathee, which is listed for hearing on 10 September 2026.

"Faith cannot be mocked under the garb of content creation. Justice is being delivered step by step."

Jai Shri Ram 🙏

Special thanks to Sr. Adv. Makarand D. Adkar Ji (@AdkarMakarand) for his guidance and support, and to the legal team for their efforts.

🚨 #FACTCHECK: Nigel Farage on Burnham, Russia and Brexit

‘Mirror, mirror, on the wall, whose claims stand up after all?’

I’m a retired academic, media literate, and equipped with critical thinking skills, so I have time to do this quickly and accurately.

Earlier today, Nigel Farage called Prime Minister Andy Burnham “a liar” over his claim that Russia interfered in the 2016 EU referendum. Here is how Farage’s statements hold up against the record.

In an interview with The Rest Is Politics  podcast, released on 12 October but widely reported the day before, Burnham said that on taking office in July he asked whether Russia had interfered in the 2016 referendum, and was given “the clear answer that yes there was.” He did not say how Russia interfered and did not publish any evidence.

This morning, Farage held a press conference in Dover, Kent, to launch Reform UK’s asylum plans. LBC’s Emma Corr asked whether Burnham’s claim tainted the result, and how Farage felt about having potentially benefited from possible Russian interference. He later repeated several of his claims in an interview with GB News.

The exchange between Corr and Farage is available on YouTube from 1:00:07: https://t.co/zJMuAlHXdx

1. “The prime minister is a liar. Yes, a liar.”

Verdict: Unsupported.

Lying means knowingly saying something false. Burnham reported advice he says he received on entering No 10. That advice has not been made public, so his claim is unverified, and critics are entitled to say so. Nothing Farage cited shows that Burnham knew it to be untrue. At most, Farage offered evidence that the claim is unproven.

2. “Boris Johnson, when he became foreign secretary, one of the first questions he asked was, ‘Was there seen to be Russian interference in the referendum campaign?’ And the answer was no.”

Verdict: Misleading.

I could find no public record of this exchange. Johnson’s recorded public position was more qualified. In Moscow in December 2017, Russian foreign minister Sergei Lavrov said Johnson had confirmed Russia had not interfered in the referendum. Johnson interrupted him: “Not successfully.” He went on to say that Russian attempts to interfere in British elections and the referendum, whatever they may have been, had not succeeded. His position was that attempts may have been made and had failed, which is a different claim from “no”.

The premise that anyone checked is also doubtful. Parliament’s Intelligence and Security Committee (ISC) published its Russia Report in July 2020. It found that the government “had not seen or sought evidence of successful interference” in UK democratic processes. It called for an intelligence assessment of the referendum, and the government refused.

In 2019, BuzzFeed reported two anonymous sources saying British intelligence had found no evidence of Russian meddling in the referendum. That claim was unverified, and the ISC’s report the following year said the government had not sought such evidence.

3. Stephen Doughty “rowed it back and said even if there was some, it made no difference.”

Verdict: Misrepresents the minister.

Doughty, a Foreign Office minister, did narrow Burnham’s claim during Monday morning’s broadcast interviews. He told LBC that Russia had attempted to interfere in the vote but had not succeeded, and made the same point to Sky News. He also said Burnham had been making a broader point about Russian attempts to interfere in democratic events in the UK and across Europe.

On the @BBC Today programme, which Farage named, Doughty spoke of Russian attempts to interfere in a range of democratic processes. He cited the jailing of former Reform UK Wales leader Nathan Gill for taking bribes to promote pro-Kremlin narratives.

Farage’s summary distorts this. “Even if there was some” turns Doughty’s acknowledgement of attempts into a hypothetical. Farage followed it with the words “There was no Russian interference,” and in his later GB News interview (see 10) he attributed that denial to Doughty himself. I found no report of Doughty’s interviews containing those words, or anything to that effect. Doughty said Russia tried to interfere.

4. “There was no Russian interference… And the Russia hoax has run all the way through this.”

Verdict: Not supported by the evidence.

No official finding says there was no interference. The government’s position since 2020 has been narrower: “We have seen no evidence of successful interference in the EU Referendum.” The ISC noted open-source studies pointing to anti-EU content on the Russian state outlets RT and Sputnik, and to the use of bots and trolls, as evidence of attempts to influence the campaign. It criticised the government for not investigating.

The defensible position is that attempts at influence were plausibly documented, their effect was never assessed, and no public evidence shows they changed the result. “No interference” and “hoax” both go well beyond that. The same standard applies to Burnham, whose “clear answer” rests on advice the public has not seen.

5. Arron Banks “was severely libelled over this. But in the end … [he] won in the high court.”

Verdict: False.

Banks sued the journalist Carole Cadwalladr over a 2019 TED Talk and a tweet. He lost in the High Court in June 2022, where the judge held that Cadwalladr’s public interest defence covered the talk. In February 2023, the Court of Appeal found partly in his favour, on one of his three grounds of appeal. It ruled that the defence lapsed for the talk’s continued publication after 29 April 2020, the date of an Electoral Commission statement clearing Banks. It upheld the dismissal of his claim over the tweet. Cadwalladr was ordered to pay £35,000 in damages and 60% of Banks’s High Court costs.

The case also had no bearing on whether Russia interfered in the referendum. It concerned Cadwalladr’s statement about Banks and “his covert relationship with the Russian Government.”

6. “I don’t think our growth figures are anything to write home about. But … they’re a damn sight better than France and Germany and Italy.”

Verdict: Accurate for this year, but selective over the longer term, and beside the point.

On current figures Farage has a case. In the second quarter of 2026, UK GDP grew by 0.5%, against 0.3% in Germany and zero in France. The IMF’s July forecasts put the UK third in the G7 for 2026, at 1%, behind the US (2.3%) and Canada (1.1%). That is ahead of Germany (0.7%), France and Japan (both 0.6%) and Italy (0.5%). The OECD’s September forecasts placed the UK joint second in the G7, level with Germany at 1.1%.

The longer view is less flattering. Between the end of 2019 and the second quarter of 2026, UK GDP grew by 6.2%, behind the eurozone as a whole (7.6%) and far behind the US (15.6%), though well ahead of Germany (1.9%, the lowest in the G7).

By naming France, Germany and Italy, Farage compared the UK with three of Europe’s weaker performers, while the eurozone overall has grown faster since the pandemic. Headline growth has also been flattered by rapid population growth. In late 2024, the Resolution Foundation found UK GDP per head still below its end-2019 level, although per-head growth picked up to 0.6% in the first quarter of 2026.

More importantly, none of these comparisons answers Burnham’s claim. Whether Brexit has done “more harm than good” depends on how the UK compares with a UK that stayed in the EU. The Office for Budget Responsibility (OBR) assumes Brexit will leave UK trade around 15% lower in the long run, and potential productivity around 4% lower, than if the UK had remained. In 2024 it said these assumptions appeared “broadly on track.”

Some economists, including Julian Jessop, a former chief economist and head of the Brexit unit at the free-market Institute of Economic Affairs, dispute these estimates.

Even so, the official forecaster’s central view is that Brexit carries a long-run cost, and growth rankings, whether flattering or not, do not settle the question.

7. “If you even look at trade numbers, the increase in trade since Brexit…”

Verdict: Partly accurate, but selective.

Total UK exports have grown since the referendum. Briefings for Britain, a pro-Brexit research group using ONS data, puts total exports in 2025 at 5% above 2019 in real terms. That growth has come from services. The House of Commons Library reports that UK services exports to the EU were 28% above their 2019 level in real terms in 2025. However, goods exports to the EU were 14% below it, having fallen in real terms in each of 2023, 2024 and 2025.

Not all of that fall is due to Brexit, but post-Brexit barriers fall mainly on goods, and goods trade with the EU is where the decline shows. The overall total obscures it.

8. Brexit has brought “some level of inconvenience… showing a passport, filling in a form,” amounting to “mild inconveniences.”

Verdict: Understatement.

Farage conceded there was more inconvenience “for people like Alcaline,” a Kent road haulage firm based near Hythe, but described it as “showing a passport, filling in a form.” The evidence suggests that undersells the effect, particularly for firms moving goods across the Channel.

In March 2024 the OBR reported that UK goods trade was around 10% below 2019 levels and growing well behind other advanced economies, while services trade had grown more strongly than in the rest of the G7. The OBR attributed the gap partly to post-Brexit barriers falling mainly on goods.

Brexit is not the only cause of the 14% real-terms fall in goods exports to the EU, but official forecasters attribute part of it to post-Brexit trade barriers, which go well beyond passports and forms. Farage’s answer also merges two separate issues: control of migration, and the trade frictions that come from leaving the single market and customs union.

9. Burnham is “looking forward to sitting down with Marine Le Pen or the AfD”

Verdict: Speculation, contrary to the record.

Farage offered no basis for this. In the interview that prompted the row, Burnham cited the German chancellor’s view that the AfD were linked to, and possibly funded by, Russia. He presented the party as a threat to European democracy.

10. The GB News version

Verdict: False.

In an interview with GB News later that day, Farage said Doughty, “being interviewed on the BBC this morning, disavowed it and said no, there was no Russian interference, it didn’t affect anything.” The “even if there was some” qualification had gone, leaving a flat denial attributed to the minister. Doughty’s reported position was that Russia attempted to interfere but did not succeed, which confirms attempted interference.

Farage also presented Johnson and Doughty together as evidence that “both Labour and Conservative camps” reject Burnham’s claim. Neither man said there was no interference. Johnson’s recorded words in 2017 were “Not successfully.” Doughty said Russia had tried and failed. What both rejected was the narrower claim that interference succeeded, which is also the extent of the official government position since 2020.

Conclusion

Farage’s sharpest claims are his weakest. Nothing presented shows that Burnham lied.

Johnson’s record says “not successfully” rather than “no”. The minister Farage cited acknowledged Russian attempts. In Dover, Farage turned that acknowledgement into a hypothetical, and on GB News into a flat denial. Banks did not win in the High Court.

Farage is on firmer ground on recent growth rankings and on total exports, though neither settles whether Brexit has helped or harmed the UK, and goods trade with the EU tells a different story.

Burnham, for his part, has made a significant claim without publishing the evidence behind it. The assessment the ISC recommended six years ago would serve the public better than either man’s certainty.

Finally, it is worth measuring Farage by his own yardstick. Farage called the British prime minister a liar. 

The evidence he offered went only to whether Burnham was wrong, not to whether he knew it. If being wrong, or being unable to prove a claim, is enough to make someone a liar, the same test can be applied to Farage.

By that standard, his answer in Dover contained five “lies”: that Johnson was told there was no interference; that Doughty conceded only that any interference “made no difference”; that there was no Russian interference; that the affair was a “hoax”; and that Arron Banks “won in the high court.”

On GB News he added a sixth, that “both Labour and Conservative camps” deny any interference, and repeated three of the others.

That makes six distinct claims, and nine in all, across two appearances in a single day. The row began over one claim by Burnham.

The fairer test, and the one this fact check applies, is that lying requires knowing a statement to be false. By that measure, nobody can say Farage lied, any more than he can say it of Burnham.

But on the evidence, Burnham’s claim remains unproven, while at least one of Farage’s, about his friend’s libel case, is plainly false on the public record.

A guy was about to tap "Buy Now" on a $299.99 espresso machine on Amazon. Full price.

His wife, a former Amazon fulfillment operations lead, took the phone out of his hands.

She scrolled 3 inches down the exact same product page. Tapped one small gray link. Same machine. Same brand. Same model. Shipped from the same Amazon warehouse. $164.19.

"How?"

"Look at the fulfillment tag. See where it says Amazon Resale: Like New? That means the outer cardboard box got dented on a delivery pallet. The $299.99 is the standard retail listing. The $164.19 is the exact same unopened machine inside a bruised box. Same return protection. Same two-day Prime truck. $135 difference. Because you only look at the yellow Buy Now button."

He looked at her.

"How long have you known this?"

"Since my first week at the fulfillment center. 5 years ago. Everything on Amazon runs on warehouse codes and pricing triggers. LPN stickers track returns. The 15th of the month forces sellers into liquidation. A simple URL code unlocks hidden 70% clearance. I've been using them for years. You've been paying retail for years."

Here's every hidden Amazon warehouse code and pricing rule and what it means for your wallet:

Code 1: "Used - Like New" under Amazon Resale. Brand new products trapped in dented cardboard at up to 40% off retail.

She said this is the single biggest pricing loophole on the entire platform, because most shoppers see the word "Used" and immediately scroll past it.

"Right below the yellow 'Buy Now' button on millions of items, there is a small box that says 'Save with Used - Like New' sold by Amazon Resale, formerly called Amazon Warehouse. Most buyers assume someone used the product at home and sent it back dirty. In the vast majority of cases for 'Like New' grade, that's completely false."

"Inside an Amazon fulfillment center, strict platform compliance rules dictate what can be sold as 'New.' If a forklift bumps a pallet and crushes the corner of a cardboard box, that item is dead as 'New' inventory. If a customer orders the wrong color, opens the outer shipping tape, sees their mistake, and drops it at UPS without ever touching the product inside, it cannot go back into the 'New' bin."

"Instead, a warehouse associate runs a quick visual grading check, sees the factory plastic seal is still intact, grades it 'Used - Like New,' and the pricing system automatically slashes the price by 25% to 50% to clear the shelf space."

"She said 'Used - Like New' and 'Used - Very Good' are how employees furnish their entire homes. 'When I worked the grading station, I watched brand-new $400 kitchen appliances, Sony headphones, and power tools get marked down by $150 simply because the cardboard box had a tear from a box cutter. The machine inside had never been plugged into a wall. Shoppers who click the yellow button pay an extra $135 just to have unwrinkled cardboard that they throw in the recycling bin ten minutes after delivery.'"

Code 2: The "LPN" Barcode Sticker. The warehouse License Plate Number that gives you instant leverage when a "New" item isn't new.

She said this three-letter code is printed on a small white sticker on millions of packages, and knowing what it means gives you immediate leverage with customer support.

"Every single item that passes through an Amazon return center gets slapped with a white barcode sticker starting with the letters 'LPN,' which stands for License Plate Number. That sticker ties the physical box to a specific return ID in Amazon's internal database, recording the return history of that exact unit."

"Here is why you need to check every box you order: fulfillment center workers move fast under intense hourly quotas. Mistakes happen constantly. A returned item with an LPN sticker occasionally gets routed back into the 'New' inventory bin by mistake."

"If you pay full retail price for a 'New' item and it arrives with a white LPN barcode sticker stuck over the original manufacturer barcode, you did not receive untouched factory inventory. You paid full price for a previously returned unit."

"When this happens, you don't have to pack it up and drive to UPS. Open the Amazon customer chat and use the exact warehouse terminology. Tell the agent: 'I paid full retail price for a New item, but the package arrived with an LPN return sticker on the box. Since I received previously returned inventory, I would like an open-box partial credit adjustment to keep it instead of returning it.'"

"She said mentioning the LPN code changes the chat conversation immediately. 'The moment you point out the LPN sticker, the support rep knows a fulfillment grading error happened. Because it costs Amazon money to ship that item back and re-grade it, support agents can offer a partial refund or promotional credit on the spot so you keep the item without triggering a return.'"

text:
Starlink already has its license in India, and taking time on the final decision is the right call by the government.

The Department of Telecommunications gave Starlink its satellite internet licence in June 2025. 

The spectrum is still pending for approval plus a second round of security clearance and FDI approval is pending.

Now, Starlink isn't the only one waiting. 

Jio's satellite arm and Airtel-backed OneWeb have the same licence and are stuck at the same step. In September, the Digital Communications Commission cleared the pricing, 5% of revenue, or 4% for rural and remote areas. 

Now it needs Cabinet approval.

The Ambani angle doesn't hold up either. 

India decided to allocate satellite spectrum directly instead of auctioning it. That's what Musk asked for and what Jio fought against. In 2025, Jio even signed a deal to sell Starlink equipment in its stores.

Elon has every reason to push. India is one of the biggest internet markets in the world. But that doesn't mean India should adhere to his timelines.

Satellite internet works differently from a normal Jio or Airtel connection. The signal comes straight from a satellite owned by a foreign company. 

Without proper checks, anyone with a dish could go online without any Indian agency knowing.

In 2024, smugglers carrying about 6,000 kg of meth used a Starlink Mini to navigate from Myanmar towards the Andamans. Andaman police had to send Starlink a legal notice asking who bought the device.

This June, Bloomberg reported the Home Ministry held back final clearance after Starlink terminals were reportedly used in the Middle East conflict, in a region where Starlink wasn't licensed. 

Starlink called that report misleading. Either way, it shows why India wants every terminal here to follow Indian rules.

Then there's control. 

In 2022, Ukraine asked Musk to turn on Starlink coverage near Crimea for a strike on Russian ships. By his own account, he said no. 

So a private businessman made a call that shaped a military operation.

India doesn't want anyone outside the country holding that switch, especially near the borders with Pakistan and China.

So India asked for data centres inside the country, lawful interception, geo-fencing in sensitive areas, and terminals that report their location. 

Jio, OneWeb and Starlink all have to meet the same rules.

Starlink will probably launch here soon. But it must happen on India's terms.

Meta must stop silently withholding the Instagram accounts of independent journalists in India

13 October 2026

Since 9 October 2026, Instagram has made the accounts of several independent journalists covering the protests in Delhi unavailable in India. Utkarsh Gaur’s main account was withheld on 9 October, and Sunny Tomar’s soon after. On the night of 12 October, Instagram withheld the account of Shubhangi Das Gupta, a 22-year-old independent journalist, and her secondary account now appears to face the same action. Today, Journo Mirror’s account was withheld in India. Each received the same notice, that Instagram had, “temporarily restricted access to this account pursuant to legal requirements under India’s Information Technology (Intermediary Guidelines and Digital Media Ethics Code) Rules.” The notice does not say which authority made the demand, which rule was invoked, which post was objected to, or when the “temporary” restriction ends. It arrives as a no-reply notification after the account has gone dark, with no prior warning and no reason.

The same day, IANS and ANI, citing Delhi Police sources, reported that around 500 posts “spreading rumours or trying to create unrest among people” had been taken down. On 12 October, PTI had put the figure at 300, which means about 200 more in one day. The police have not said which posts were removed, from which platforms, under which provision, or whether anyone who posted them was told. We are also receiving reports of WhatsApp accounts being shut down and of mobile numbers being put through fresh KYC verification that leaves them unusable while it is pending. All of this comes alongside a timeline in which there was suspension of internet services and public transport in the heart of the national capital.

IFF condemns Meta’s withholding of entire journalist accounts on the strength of an unnamed “legal requirement”, and the Delhi Police’s practice of announcing a running censorship tally through anonymous sources. Meta must restore these accounts, tell every affected user who asked for the restriction and under what law, and stop turning demands about particular posts into the silencing of entire accounts.
The IT Rules, 2021, on which Meta’s notice relies, give it two routes to restrict content. The notice meets the conditions of neither. If Meta acted on a government demand, the route is Rule 3(1)(d). If Meta acted on its own, Rule 4(8) requires it, as a significant social media intermediary, to notify the user before disabling access, explain the grounds, and give an adequate opportunity to dispute the action. None of this happened. In this situation at present the entire burden will be shifted to the user to seek remedy under Rules 3(2) and 3A, where a user must first go to Meta’s Grievance Officer, who has 15 days, and then to the Grievance Appellate Committee, which has 30 more. In our experience these timelines are often not met, and a grievance against unnamed “legal requirements” is likely to be answered by pointing back to them. Whatever the intention, the effect is to keep a journalist off the platform for more than six weeks, exactly when her reporting matters most.

The Delhi Police figures raise their own questions. “Rumour” is not a ground for restricting speech under Article 19(2).  A count of 500 posts announced through unnamed sources does not let anyone tell whether a post was fabricated or simply showed something the police did not want seen. Nor is it obvious that 200 reasoned intimations, each signed by an officer of DIG rank and each identifying the provision, the unlawful act and the exact URL, were issued in a single day.

Our demands

1) Meta should restore every account withheld in connection with the protests where the underlying demand, if any, concerned specific posts, and restrict no more than the URLs named in a lawful reasoned intimation.
2) Meta should tell each affected user in writing which authority made the demand, the issuing officer’s rank, the provision relied on, the content identified, and when the restriction will end.
3) Meta should disclose whether its systems automatically extend demands about individual posts to entire accounts, and stop any such escalation immediately.
4) The Delhi Police should publish the takedown requests it has issued, with their number, platforms, provisions, issuing officers and reasons, as Anuradha Bhasin requires.
5) MeitY should ensure notice and a hearing to every person whose content is restricted, publish the outcome of the monthly Secretary-level review under Rule 3(1)(d), and stop using Section 79(3)(b), the Sahyog Portal and “temporary” restrictions under the IT Rules to bypass the safeguards of Section 69A.
If you have been affected

If your post or account was withheld or removed in connection with the protests, or you received a notice about a police data request, write to legal@internetfreedom.in for pro bono assistance. Keep screenshots of every notice, note the date and time, and delete nothing. Document, document, document.
