text: i went to collect my repaired laptop on friday, and the technician asked me whether i'd backed up my files before bringing it in. i said yes, then he asked why i'd deleted a folder called "march" the night before. i told him i hadn't touched the laptop since dropping it off four days earlier. he turned the screen towards me. the folder was gone, but the activity log showed it had been opened and deleted at 11:42 pm the previous night. i asked whether someone had accessed my laptop remotely. he said the laptop had been disconnected from the internet while they worked on it. then he showed me something else. at 11:39 pm, someone had created a new user account using my full name. i told him to check the security camera. he did, then stopped the video and asked me to look at the person sitting at the repair desk. it was me. same face, same clothes, same scar above my eyebrow. except i'd been at home that night, and my wife had watched me fall asleep beside her.

text: i watched the footage again, and this time i noticed the man had a bandage around his right thumb. i'd cut mine badly opening a tin the day before i dropped the laptop off. the technician called the police, and they checked the sign-in records. someone had collected a spare key from the reception desk using a collection slip with my signature, entered the shop after closing, and used the laptop's local account to delete the folder. the technician had forgotten to lock the back entrance after taking out the rubbish, so the person hadn't needed to break in. the police found the collection slip in the bin. the signature was copied from the repair form i'd signed four days earlier. the folder contained scanned documents from my divorce proceedings, including a financial statement i'd never shown anyone. i called my wife and asked whether she'd sent someone to the shop. she denied it, then admitted she'd asked my brother to retrieve a file from my laptop before the technician returned it. she'd told him the folder contained photographs she wanted deleted, not legal documents. my brother had agreed because he thought he was helping us avoid another argument. he'd used my clothes and a cap from my car to make himself look like me on the camera, but he hadn't realised the bandage would make him easier to identify. the part that changed everything was the file he hadn't managed to delete: a draft email addressed to my lawyer, written from my account, offering to withdraw my claim to the house. my wife had planned to send it after the folder was gone, then tell me i'd agreed to settle. she hadn't needed to forge my signature on the legal documents. she only needed me to believe i'd changed my mind. my brother confessed when the police showed him the footage. he said he'd done it to keep our family together. i asked him which family he meant, and he couldn't answer.

By Skye Jacobs  Today 2:36 PM    
Your ChatGPT conversations could end up in court, and they're not protected
Chatbot conversations lack the legal privilege covering communications with lawyers, doctors, and therapists

 Add TechSpot 
   📷
Serving tech enthusiasts for over 25 years.  
 TechSpot means tech analysis and advice you can trust.
The takeaway: Private  conversations with AI chatbots are increasingly being used in court  cases, creating a new source of evidence for police, prosecutors, and  civil litigants. These records can expose a user's intentions, private  thoughts, and sensitive disclosures, yet they generally receive none of  the legal confidentiality protections afforded to conversations with  lawyers, doctors, or therapists.
ChatGPT and similar tools are often used for personal questions, legal worries, health concerns, and emotional support. Those conversations can feel private, but they may be accessible through a phone search, a  subpoena, discovery in a lawsuit, or a report by the AI company itself.

A review by The Washington Post found chatbot conversations cited in  12 public court cases over the past two years. The number is likely  higher because much of the evidence collected during investigations and  lawsuits never becomes public.

One case involved a teenager identified in court records as R.K.C.,  who sued Meta, Snap, TikTok, and YouTube in 2023. He alleged that their  platforms contributed to social media addiction and mental health  problems.

Defense lawyers obtained his ChatGPT history during the case. In one  October 2024 conversation, R.K.C. asked the chatbot to explain a  statement from his father about a possible settlement.

"My dad Said that I'm will get a settlement worth of  1million dollar," he wrote. "He said that If that doesn't make me happy  what does. What does he mean."

// Related Stories

 Ring rolls out new encryption system that could limit what it can hand over to police 
 AI is driving an "expertise recession" as people increasingly question professional advice 

R.K.C.'s lawyers settled with Snap, TikTok, and YouTube by late July.  They also dropped the case against Meta, saying they were concerned  about putting the teenager through a long trial. The companies denied  his claims. Mike Morgan, a partner at Morgan & Morgan, said the  ChatGPT messages did not affect the outcome of the case.
📷

Credit: The Washington Post

Morgan said young people may share more with a  chatbot than they would with family members, friends, or therapists. "A  fifteen-year-old may type things into a chatbot that he may not say to a  therapist, a parent, or a friend, and he does it without realizing that  it could end up in a defense expert's report," he said in a statement.

Chatbot records have also become part of criminal cases.

In Palm Beach County, Florida, OpenAI contacted the  FBI after a ChatGPT user repeatedly described plans to harm an  ex-girlfriend, according to a police affidavit. The FBI passed the  information to local police, who identified the woman and found that the  user, Darren Zhou, had sent her anonymous messages after their  relationship ended.

Police said the ChatGPT conversations supported the  credibility of the threats. Zhou was arrested in May and charged with  stalking and making electronic threats. He pleaded guilty this month and  was sentenced to eight years of probation.

OpenAI has said it uses software to detect  conversations that may involve dangerous behavior. Those conversations  can be reviewed by staff. If reviewers determine there is "an imminent  and credible risk of harm to others," the company may contact law  enforcement.

The company has not said how often it makes such  reports. Its transparency data, however, shows a sharp increase in  government and law-enforcement requests for user information. OpenAI  disclosed data from more than 80 accounts during the second half of  2025, more than four times the total from the same period a year  earlier.

In many cases, police do not need to obtain records from an AI company. They find the conversations on a person's phone.

Michael Price, litigation director of the Fourth  Amendment Center at the National Association of Criminal Defense  Lawyers, said people often agree to let officers search their phones. In  most situations, people have the right to refuse a search unless police  have a warrant.

"The short answer is that most people consent," Price told The Washington Post. "They shouldn't, but they do."

📷

That happened in the case of Ryan Schaefer, a  Missouri State University student accused of damaging 17 cars in a  campus parking lot. According to police records, Schaefer agreed to let  officers search his phone. They found ChatGPT messages he sent shortly  after the alleged vandalism.

"How f----d am i bro," Schaefer wrote. "What if i smahsed the s--- oitta mutlipls cars."

He later wrote: "Is there any way they could know it was me."

Schaefer later pleaded guilty to felony property damage and was sentenced in July to five years of probation.

AI chats can also be pulled into civil lawsuits  through the discovery process. In a Michigan employment case, a tire  salesman's former employer alleged that he had taken customers after  joining a rival company. The salesman had asked ChatGPT whether deleted  Yahoo emails could still be retrieved, including through a court  subpoena.

The employer argued that the messages showed he had  tried to hide evidence. A judge later ordered him to pay an undetermined  amount in attorneys' fees and allowed the lawsuit to continue.

Chatbot exchanges do not have the legal protections  that apply to conversations with lawyers, doctors, or therapists. OpenAI  CEO Sam Altman has said AI conversations should have stronger privacy  protections because people increasingly use chatbots for sensitive  matters. Courts have not recognized that type of privilege.

A federal judge in New York made that clear in a case  involving financial executive Bradley Heppner. Heppner argued that  prosecutors should not be allowed to review his conversations with  Anthropic's Claude about potential fraud defenses. The judge ruled that  the chats were not protected because Claude is not a lawyer and  Heppner's attorneys had not told him to consult the chatbot.

Heppner was convicted in May of securities fraud, wire fraud, and other charges.

The issue may grow as AI tools take on more tasks for  users and gain access to more personal data. Andrew Ferguson, a law  professor at George Washington University who studies digital  surveillance, said chatbot records may be only the beginning.

"Your entire world is going to now be available for police," Ferguson said.

text:
A Black family with two rooms and six children fed a stranger they could not afford to feed. It was raining in the Alabama swamp in November of 1959, and the stranger was John Howard Griffin, a white writer moving through the South with his skin chemically darkened. That night was his own daughter's fifth birthday, and he walked outside so those six children would not hear a grown man crying.

He had the rag in his hand before he ever looked up. The shoes were familiar, and Sterling Williams had knelt over that exact pair on that exact patch of French Quarter sidewalk more than once, so he knew the wear on that leather the way you know a voice through a wall.

The man standing in them was not familiar. That man had been white.

So Sterling kept working and said nothing, because saying something was not a thing a Black shoeshine man did on Royal Street in November of 1959, not to a stranger and not about a stranger's face. Then the customer asked if there was anything familiar about those shoes.

Yeah, Sterling said. He had been shining a pair like that for a white man.

Fellow named Griffin, the customer said.

Yeah. You know him?

I am him.

The man in the shoes was John Howard Griffin, a Texas writer who had just spent four days flat on his back in a borrowed New Orleans house, cotton pads over his eyes, a sunlamp burning down on him, swallowing heavy doses of a drug prescribed for vitiligo. His skin came out dark and blotchy, so he painted over the pale patches with vegetable dye and shaved his head down to the scalp.

When he finally reached over and flipped on the bathroom light, he wrote that a stranger looked back at him out of the glass, and that what he felt first was not fear. It was loneliness.

Everything about him had changed except his shoes.

That is the part nobody ever tells you about this story. The disguise held for six weeks across four states, and it held because an old Black man on a French Quarter sidewalk decided to keep his mouth shut, and then decided to teach a stranger how to stay alive.

Sterling Williams was gray-headed, a veteran of the First World War, working a corner stand with a partner named Joe. He listened to the whole crazy confession, and he laughed, and then he got practical.

He pointed at Griffin's hands. The hair on the back of them was still brown, because Griffin had darkened his face and his scalp and his forearms and never once thought about the backs of his own hands, which is exactly the kind of thing a man does not think about until his life depends on it.

Griffin dug a razor out of his duffel bag and went looking for a washroom to shave them in, and he nearly walked into the white one. Two days into being Black in Louisiana, moving fast, he had already forgotten which door was his.

Every Black man on that street had learned that reflex as a child and had never once in his life been allowed to lose it.

Sterling let him work the stand. He taught him when to smile, when to laugh, when to shrug, and when to say nothing at all, which was most of the time, and he taught him how to hold his face while a white man talked over his head.

The white customers who were friendliest, Griffin noticed, were the ones asking a Black man where they could find Black women. Sterling had a line ready for that one, which was that when they want to sin, they're very democratic.

At the end of the day the old man dished out raccoon stew at the stand, and Griffin sat there and reported back what he had found out, which was only ever what Sterling had known his entire life. Nobody in that city was going to hire a Black man to do anything but pick something up and set it down.

Sterling had been listening to men say that for forty years.

He let the new one say it anyway.

Now here is the thing that got buried under ten million book covers. The experiment was not Griffin's idea first, and it was not a white man's idea at all.

That fall he had been stuck on an article for Sepia, the Black magazine published out of Fort Worth, about the suicide rate among Black Southerners. He mailed questionnaires to Black professionals all over the South, and the few that came back came back blank.

Not hostile. Blank.

He carried his frustration to Adelle Jackson, Sepia's editorial director, a Black woman who had come up through that company from a secretary's desk to become one of the most respected editors in the country. He wanted to know why they would not talk to him when he was on their side.

She did not soften it.

Black people knew that no matter how hard he tried he would never understand, she told him, and the only way he was ever going to know what it was like was to be one.

He drove home with that sentence sitting in his chest and it did not leave. When he came back later and told her what he intended to do, she looked at him and said he did not know what he was getting into.

Then she laid out, years before any of it happened, exactly what it would cost him and his wife and his children. She was right about every single part of it.

She got one paragraph.

He rode a Greyhound out of New Orleans into Mississippi. Seven months earlier a mob had taken Mack Charles Parker out of his cell in the Poplarville jail three days before his trial and left him in the Pearl River.

The FBI put together a file running around three hundred and seventy pages with confessions inside it, and a county grand jury of eighteen white men read it and declined to charge anybody. That was the state Griffin bought a ticket into, and everybody Black on that bus understood it better than he did.

At a rest stop the driver swung the door open and let the white passengers off to use the restrooms. Then he turned around and told the Black passengers to stay in their seats.

They said something about it, and they stayed anyway.

Griffin sat there doing the arithmetic every one of them had done a thousand times, which is how many more miles until a man is allowed to relieve himself.

Then there was the stare. He called it the hate stare, and he wrote that it landed on him like a blow, out of bus stations and store counters and passing cars, from people who had never met him and never would.

He had lived forty years in the South and had never once been on the receiving end of it. Ten of those years he had been blind.

He lost his sight in the Pacific in 1945, from shrapnel in an air raid, and did not get it back until one afternoon in January of 1957, when the redness swirled and he stumbled into the house and called his wife and started crying into the telephone. He had written, during that decade in the dark, that a blind man can only take the measure of another man's heart and mind, and that neither one of those tells you a thing about his color.

Then he got his eyes back and joined the rest of us.

He hitchhiked out of Mobile toward Montgomery, and most of the white men who stopped for him wanted to talk about one subject, and it was not the weather. One farmer patted the shotgun leaning against his knee, nodded at the swamp running along both sides of the road, and explained how easy it would be for a Black man to go in there and never be asked about again.

Griffin said yes sir, and got out at the next chance, and walked. He walked for hours in the heat until he reached a roadside store where an old white couple first turned him away, then looked at the state of him and let him buy a meal, then watched him eat it like he might take the plate with him.

It was late and raining by the time a young Black man in a mill truck pulled over for him. The man worked at a sawmill, and on the drive he explained to Griffin how the arrangement actually functioned down there, which was that a Black man was never permitted to pay a debt all the way off.

You stayed a little behind forever, and a man who is a little behind forever does what he is told. Then the driver asked Griffin where he was sleeping that night, and Griffin admitted he did not know, and the man took him home.

Home was two rooms on the edge of the swamp.

There was a wife inside and six children, and there was nothing.

Griffin looked around at what that family did not have, and then watched them make room for a stranger inside it. They fed him out of a pot that was not big enough for the people already in the house, and the children crowded him and looked him over and decided he was fine.

The parents put him where they could put him, and in a house that size there is no privacy for anybody and nobody pretends there is. Then everybody went to sleep on pallets on the floor.

It was the nineteenth of November. Back in Texas, Griffin's daughter Susie was five years old that day.

He lay in the dark in that two-room house and thought about the candles and the cake and the party dress, and about his sons in their good suits, all of them asleep in clean beds in a warm house. Then he got up and went out into the swamp so the children would not hear him, and he stood in the rain and cried.

What broke him was not what had been done to him that week.

It was arithmetic.

Those six children were the same as his six-year-old and his five-year-old and his baby in every way a human being actually is. The only difference on the table was the pigment in their skin, the least important fact about any child ever born, and that one fact was going to decide everything that happened to them for the rest of their lives.

He understood, standing out there in the rain, that if his own children had that skin this country would have handed them those same two rooms without blinking, and called it fair.

A few nights later, with no room anywhere, an old Black preacher took him in and shared a thin mattress with him in a small bare room. They lay under the quilts looking at the ceiling and talking about miracles.

The old man loved the one about Lazarus coming up out of the grave, and he could go on about that for a long time. Then Griffin asked him what he thought the future held for Black people in the South, and the old man's certainty went out of him.

He had two sons.

They had gone north, and he said he hoped they never came back.

A father in Alabama, praying his boys stayed a thousand miles away from him until the day he died, because that was the best thing he could picture for them.

In Montgomery, Griffin stopped taking the pills for a few days and scrubbed at the dye until his skin came up light enough. Then he walked into a whites-only restaurant, ordered a meal, and got smiled at.

Afterward he put the dye back on and crossed back over. He did that on purpose, back and forth across the same city, testing whether the line was really that simple.

It was.

The only thing he ever changed was the color, and it changed everything, every single time.

But look at what he was doing. He was choosing.

That is the whole distance between him and every other person in this story.

Now go home with him, and go back three years. Griffin lived in Mansfield, Texas, a farm town of about fifteen hundred people seventeen miles south of Fort Worth.

He did not have to go to Louisiana to find out what this country did to Black people.

He could have walked downtown.

In 1955 a Fort Worth attorney named L. Clifford Davis filed a federal lawsuit for the Mansfield NAACP on behalf of three Black teenagers, and their names were Floyd Moody, his cousin Charles Moody, and Nathaniel Jackson.

Every school morning they walked down to the little drugstore around seven and caught a Trailways bus into Fort Worth, eight or ten Black kids at a time. The only high school in the county that would take them was I. M. Terrell, twenty blocks past where that bus let them out.

The white high school was in their own town.

In August of 1956 the Fifth Circuit ruled that keeping them out on account of their race was unlawful, the first time a federal court had ordered a Texas school district to desegregate. Mansfield answered within days.

Crosses were burned in the Black neighborhood on the twenty-second and the twenty-third of August. Floyd Moody's father, J. E. Moody, worked land he did not own, and the white man who owned it told him that if he sent that boy to that school, you're going to have to move.

He was put off the place. T. M. Moody, who helped lead the whole effort, had his agreement to draw well water cancelled by the school district, and then word got around that somebody meant to kill him.

When the police made it clear they were not going to sit outside his house, Black men from the neighborhood armed themselves and did it instead.

On the morning of August 30, 1956, a crowd began gathering at Mansfield High School. By the time it was finished there were somewhere between two hundred and five hundred white people standing on that campus, and over the next several days they came back twice more.

They hung three effigies of Black people.

One was strung on wires across Main Street downtown, one went up on the flagpole in front of the school, and one was hung directly over the front entrance so that white students walked underneath it to get to class.

A photographer got a picture of Texas Rangers standing in that yard with the thing hanging in the frame behind them. A sign on one of the figures said this would be a terrible way to die.

Cars were parked around the school with threats and slurs painted across them. A local man named John Pyles stood in that crowd holding a baby alligator up where everybody could see it, and the joke, if you can call it that, was that any Black child who set foot on that campus was gator bait.

Governor Allan Shivers sent in the Texas Rangers, and their orders were not to walk those three young men through the door. Their orders were to remove any Black student who tried to enroll, and Shivers said publicly that he would not use the state's officers against citizens making an orderly protest.

The effigy stayed hanging over the school entrance.

Nobody in a badge took it down.

Floyd Moody was sixteen years old, and he remembered that when they left the school that day everything had seemed all right, and that by evening everybody in the city had heard. No Black student registered at Mansfield High School in 1956.

None registered the next year either, or the year after that. The district stayed segregated until 1965, nine full years after a federal court told it to stop, and Floyd A Black family with two rooms and six children fed a stranger they could not afford to feed. It was raining in the Alabama swamp in November of 1959, and the stranger was John Howard Griffin, a white writer moving through the South with his skin chemically darkened. That night was his own daughter's fifth birthday, and he walked outside so those six children would not hear a grown man crying.

Moody finished his junior and senior years riding that bus into Fort Worth.

John Howard Griffin was living on a farm outside that town the whole time. He was blind that August and could not have seen those effigies if he had walked directly under them.

He got his sight back the following January.

Two and a half years after that he was lying in a New Orleans bathroom under a sunlamp, trying to find out what it was like.

The Sepia articles ran starting in April of 1960 under the title Journey into Shame. Six thousand letters came in and only nine of them were hostile, which tells you something about this country's private conscience and absolutely nothing about its public one.

Then Mansfield answered again. One night that April somebody hung an effigy of Griffin beside the downtown traffic light, half of it painted black and half of it white, with a yellow stripe running down the back.

The same town, the same downtown, four years apart.

A few days later a cross was burned in front of Mansfield's Black elementary school. That had nothing to do with Griffin and everything to do with who was actually expected to pay for what he wrote.

Anonymous callers told him what they were going to do to him when they came, and his father came over and sat up in the house with a shotgun across his lap. Griffin sent his wife and their four children to Mexico, his parents sold their property and followed, and he came behind them and stayed nine months, and that is where he finished the book.

He got out. The children at that elementary school did not.

It had all happened once already, eleven years earlier, and America managed to forget it completely.

In May of 1948 Ray Sprigle, a Pulitzer winner at the Pittsburgh Post-Gazette, tanned himself for three weeks in Florida, shaved his head, took the name James Crawford, and rode through the Jim Crow South for thirty days. He drew up a fresh will before he left, and his twenty-one part series ran on front pages and started the first real national argument about segregation in this country.

He did not do it alone, and he could not have. The NAACP put him with John Wesley Dobbs of Atlanta, who was sixty-six years old, the son of a man born in slavery, grand master of Georgia's Black Masons, the unofficial mayor of Auburn Avenue and a neighbor of a preacher's boy named Martin.

Dobbs drove them roughly three thousand miles in his 1947 Mercury. He took that white reporter down into the Delta, into the homes of sharecroppers and Black doctors, into the front rooms of families whose men had been lynched, and he introduced him everywhere as his cousin.

If that cover had broken, Sprigle would have gone home to Pittsburgh.

Dobbs would have been left standing in Mississippi.

Sprigle never printed his name. He left it out on purpose to protect him, and it worked, and it also meant that the man who made the entire thing possible became a blank space in his own story.

The public did not learn what John Wesley Dobbs had done until 1998. He died on August 30, 1961, the same week Atlanta's public schools were finally desegregated, about six weeks before Black Like Me arrived in American bookstores under one man's name.

That book sold more than ten million copies. It went into fourteen languages, got made into a movie, and has been assigned in American high schools for six decades.

Every word in it was something Black people had already been saying out loud, in print, from pulpits and witness stands and front porches, for as long as anybody could remember. The historian Nell Irvin Painter said it plainly, that when Griffin walked into a tense city he said the exact same thing local Black people had been saying for years, and the only difference was that the men in charge could hear it coming out of him.

That is the buried truth in this story, and it is not a compliment to anybody.

Griffin understood it eventually. Stokely Carmichael called it an excellent book for white people, and Griffin agreed with him, and in time he mostly quit lecturing on it, saying it was absurd for a white man to presume to speak for Black people when they have superlative voices of their own.

Now, the rumor. For over forty years people have passed around the story that the drug got him in the end, that he died of skin cancer he earned by turning himself Black.

People repeat it because it lands like justice or like tragedy depending on who is telling it. It is not true and it never was.

He never had skin cancer, and the drug gave him nausea and fatigue and nothing worse than that. He died in Fort Worth on September 9, 1980, at sixty years old, of complications from diabetes, at the end of a body already taken apart by a war injury, spinal malaria, ten years of blindness, an amputated leg and a run of heart attacks.

When a friend asked his wife what had finally killed him, she did not give a diagnosis.

Here is what the record kept. A title borrowed off a Langston Hughes poem, a movie, ten million copies, and one name on the cover.

Here is what the record misplaced. Adelle Jackson, who supplied the idea and got a paragraph, and John Wesley Dobbs, who drove that same road eleven years earlier at sixty-six and waited half a century to be named for it.

Floyd Moody, Charles Moody and Nathaniel Jackson, who wanted the high school in their own town and got a mob, a burned cross, and a father put off his land. A sawmill worker with two rooms and six children who fed a stranger in the rain and never learned who he was.

And a gray-headed man on Royal Street who recognized a pair of shoes, said nothing, and then pointed at a stranger's hands.

Your people already knew what was in that book. Your grandmother could have written it and never needed a sunlamp to do it.

So when this one comes back around your feed dressed up as one brave man's adventure, put the rest of them back into it. They are the reason it exists.

In December, Griffin came back to New Orleans one last time and stood again at the stand on Royal Street. On the fourteenth he took the last dose, and over the next few days the color went out of him.

He kept the shoes.

He was the only man in the whole story who got to take something off.

I asked Qwen 3.8 max this exact question about men just 100% quitting society, jobs and all about a week ago. This is it's response. 

Your dream of when men are gone is total bs and does not show the extent of how bad it actually will get. 

This is a good thought experiment, and the answer is less about "Western civilization" in the abstract than about buffer depth — how many days of slack sit between each essential system and the people who keep it running. Let me ground the numbers before I speculate.

Let me pull the actual BLS occupational table rather than rely on remembered percentages.

Short answer: the visible economy is dead in about 72 hours. Life-critical systems fail inside a week to ten days. Population-level mass death in dense cities starts around week three to six. "Civilization coming to a screeching halt" isn't a single moment — it's a set of buffers draining at different rates, and the shortest buffer sets the pace.

First, a correction to your numbers, because a few are wrong in a direction that strengthens your case rather than weakening it.

I pulled the actual BLS table (2025 annual averages). Transportation isn't "over 80%" male — heavy and tractor-trailer truck drivers are 92.3% male. Refuse collectors are 87.3%. Construction laborers 95.3%. Electricians 96.5%. Welders 94.2%. Power plant operators and stationary engineers 95.9%. Water and wastewater treatment operators 91.7%. Aircraft pilots 93.0%. Firefighters 94.9%. General maintenance and repair workers 94.8%. Police 83.6%. Air traffic controllers were suppressed in the table, but the FAA figure is roughly four-fifths male. Farmers and agricultural managers 74.3% — the lowest number in the critical set, and still nearly three-quarters.

So on the layer that physically holds the country up — power, water, fuel, freight, construction, maintenance, waste, field telecom, manufacturing, emergency response — your "95 to 100%" is essentially correct, and in a couple of cases you understated it. Where it falls apart is the blanket claim about "most jobs." Registered nurses are 87.3% female. Elementary and secondary teachers are majority female. Cashiers are about 68% female. Office and administrative support is roughly three-quarters female. Cooks split closer, 56% male. Physicians are now only 58% male.

That asymmetry produces the single most uncomfortable feature of this scenario, and it's not the one people usually imagine.

The strike doesn't remove the caretakers. It removes the substrate they stand on. You would have fully-staffed hospitals with no electricity, no generator diesel after day four, no drug deliveries, no water pressure, and no surgeons or respiratory coverage. Fully-staffed schools with no food and no heat. Grocery stores fully staffed and completely empty. The people whose job is to hold the line would be present at work with nothing to hold it with. That's worse than if everyone had left, because it means the response capacity is intact in headcount and total in effect. Nobody is at the wheel.

Here's how the buffers drain.

Hours 0–12. Power is the first domino, because the grid is a real-time balance machine with essentially zero storage. Control rooms go unstaffed, automatic protection trips units, and each trip pushes more load onto fewer generators. Nuclear — about a fifth of US generation — scrams itself safely on loss of staffing, which is the good news and also an immediate 20% hole. Coal and gas follow as alarms go unanswered. Wind and solar run themselves for a while, which is the only mercy in the first day. Cascading regional blackouts inside 24 hours is a reasonable expectation, not a worst case. Aviation goes to a national ground stop within hours; airborne aircraft get down as fast as controllers can be found.

Days 1–3. Refineries shut down, since they need continuous staffing. Stations run dry — a typical US store holds roughly a month of sales in thirty to forty thousand gallons, which is two or three days of panic-buying turnover. Trucking stops, and trucking moves about 70% of US freight tonnage. Grocery restocking ends immediately. Water and wastewater pumping is heavily automated, so it limps along on inertia and tank levels, but chemical dosing and operator response stop; pressure failures begin within a day or two and sewage starts overflowing. Cell sites have four to eight hours of battery and a generator that nobody will refuel. Police and fire are on strike too, so 911 is a dead line from the first morning.

Days 3–7. This is where it stops being an inconvenience and starts being a body count. Hospitals hit the wall at 96 hours — that's the Joint Commission standard for backup fuel capacity, and it exists precisely because four days was judged survivable with resupply. Resupply isn't coming. Ventilator patients, ICU, neonatal, and dialysis — dialysis patients need treatment every two to three days and die within a week to ten days without it. Insulin loses cold chain. Potable water fails in cities, and dehydration becomes the leading cause of death for infants and the elderly. Looting in dense urban areas starts within 24 to 72 hours; that's the consistent pattern in every major blackout, and there is no one to respond.

Weeks 2–4. Household food averages out to one to two weeks and is very unevenly distributed — cities have almost none. Livestock in confinement is the quiet catastrophe: millions of broilers, dairy cattle, and hogs require daily water, feed, and milking. Confined animal die-off within three to seven days. Unmilked dairy cows develop mastitis in days. If the strike lands in spring planting or fall harvest, you lose a full year of food supply regardless of what happens next.

Weeks 4+. Famine mortality in dependent urban populations rises steeply. The long-tail hazard is nuclear spent fuel pools, which need cooling and have weeks to months of passive margin — recoverable if people return, genuinely bad if they don't.

Who dies, in order: ICU and ventilator patients first, inside days. Dialysis patients by day seven to ten. Insulin-dependent diabetics in week one to two as cold chain fails. Infants and elderly from dehydration in week one to two. Then starvation from week three onward. The great majority of early deaths are among people who cannot act on their own behalf — which is why this scenario is worse than a simple "the economy stops" story.

Geography decides survival more than preparation does. Rural and small-town areas with private wells, propane tanks, wood heat, gardens, and local production can hold for months. Dense cities are pure consumption nodes with two or three days of everything and no way to produce more.

Two things your framing doesn't account for that change the shape of the answer.

Recovery is not a switch. If the strike ended on day thirty, power plants need weeks of careful thermal restart, not a flip. Refineries take weeks to bring back safely. Water mains need flushing and rechlorination before they're drinkable — otherwise you get a disease wave after the crisis ends. Food needs a full growing season. And if skilled tradespeople died in the interval, the loss is generational: you cannot train a journeyman lineman or a water treatment operator in months, which is exactly why there is no backfill path. Substitution is the ceiling here — the workforce that remains could not absorb even 20% of these roles within a year, because the training pipeline is measured in years and the credentialing and physical demands are hard constraints.

And the mirror case is worth stating, because it's where the real analytical content lives. If every woman went on strike instead, the physical infrastructure would keep running for months — power, water, fuel, freight, food all stay up. What collapses is nursing, childcare, elder care, teaching, and the administrative layer, and the damage lands on a timescale of months to years rather than days to weeks, in the form of a care-sector and demographic catastrophe. So the asymmetry isn't symmetric: a men's strike kills the body fast, a women's strike kills the future slowly. Your scenario is the one with the short fuse.

What I'd flag as genuinely unknown: the exact sequence of grid collapse depends on interconnection topology and how much wind, solar, and storage is running at that hour, so the 24-hour blackout estimate is inferred rather than proven. Grocery inventory days is a widely cited figure but I couldn't source a clean authoritative number for it tonight. And the whole thing assumes total participation, which is the premise doing most of the work — a 90% strike would be catastrophic but survivable, because the remaining 10% could triage the highest-value systems for a while.

The honest bottom line: the US doesn't degrade gracefully, because it was optimized for efficiency rather than resilience. Every buffer is short by design. The failure arrives at the speed of the shortest one, and the shortest one is the electrical grid at a matter of hours.

text:
Honourable Chief Minister Shri A Revanth Reddy attended " The Hindu Huddle " session titled "By, For, and Of the People: Good Governance for Telangana" in Bengaluru on Saturday. 

During conservation with The Hindu Director N Ram, CM Revanth Reddy delved into his political journey from ZPTC member to CM, women empowerment,  job recruitment, political fight with opposition parties, Congress party’s stand on women's reservation.  Union government's indifference towards  Southern India,  Rythu Bharosa, Telangana Rising etc. 

Honourable Chief Minister Shri A @revanth_anumula  alleged that Prime Minister Narendra Modi resorted to  political gimmicks  on women's reservations in the Legislative bodies. The Congress party was opposed  to linking the women reservation to the increase of  MP seats.  If parliamentary seats are increased as proposed raising Lok Sabha seats in Kerala from 20 to 30 and in Uttar Pradesh from 80 to 120. It would be unjust and this is precisely what we oppose.

WOMEN RESERVATION AND DISCRIMINATION AGAINST SOUTHERN STATES :  

The Congress was demanding the centre not to penalize the performing southern states which  contribute significantly more to the Centre than they receive. The President, Prime Minister, and Union Home Minister all hail from northern states. The 2027 Uttar Pradesh elections are approaching and the centre should prove their sincerity in the implementation of the Women's Reservation Bill in the state first.  The Chief Minister appealed to the centre to stop widening the rift between the North and the South parts of the states.

We are the architects of women's reservation policies. Congress governments appointed women Presidents, Lok Sabha Speaker, Governors, and Chief Ministers. Rajiv Gandhi ensured representation for women in local bodies. We passed the Women's Reservation Bill in the Rajya Sabha under Sonia Gandhi's leadership.

VISIT TO CHINA SOON : 

Referring to the investments, the Chief Minister said that Gujarat was not naturally attracting investments, which are being forced into the state.  For the past 20 years, there has been just one brand ambassador working there. Telangana state was not alone competing with neighbouring states and also with the world. Why compete with neighbours only ? We are competing with China, Japan, South Korea, and Germany. My motto is 'China+1'. I visited China 15 years ago and had no hesitation in learning from anyone. I will visit China soon to learn. I once took a ten-day course at Harvard; similarly, I will visit China to understand their best practices.

BLUE COLLAR JOBS AND RECRUITMENT IN GOVERNMENT : 

On the creation of jobs,  CM Revanth Reddy said that blue-collar jobs are an alternative to white-collar jobs. AI has not created an alternative to blue-collar jobs. AI can create many things, but it cannot create a politician. Our youth need to focus on alternatives and enhance their skills. Those who had the opportunity to govern the state in the past viewed themselves merely as rulers; I, however, consider myself a public representative here to serve. There are 2 lakh vacant government jobs in Telangana and his government started recruitment. We provided 67,760 jobs in just 15 months—the highest number of jobs provided anywhere in the country. We issued notifications two weeks ago, and a notification for the recruitment of 5,000 police personnel will be issued soon. Our youth are now preparing for these jobs. The recruitment agency Telangana Public Service Commission was also revamped. During KCR rule, an RMP doctor served as a member of the commission and interviewed Group-1 candidates. Is an RMP doctor the right person to oversee appointments for engineers, doctors, and other professional roles?. the CM averred.

TELANGANA RISING 2047  :

 Elaborating the comprehensive plan for Telangana development  to achieve a $1 trillion economy by 2034 and a $3 trillion economy by 2047, the CM said that the state has been divided into 3 zones. The urban area within the 160-km Outer Ring Road (ORR) as CURE (Core Urban Region Economy),  the area between the ORR and the Regional Ring Road (RRR) is called PURE (Peri-Urban Region Economy) and beyond the RRR as RARE (Rural Agricultural Region Economy). We held a global summit on December 7, 8, and 9 last year and released a policy document. We are prioritizing the service sector in CURE, manufacturing in PURE, and agriculture in RARE. We intend to transform CURE into a 'Net Zero' city and are implementing plans aligned with this policy. Even though we are incurring an annual loss of ₹2,000 crore, we decided to mandate the use of electric vehicles (EVs) within the CURE zone and waived taxes on EVs.  We are undertaking Metro expansion and restoring lakes by removing encroachments. Constructing water harvesting wells and promoting the manufacturing sector within the region and also  building 'Bharat Future City' across 30,000 acres and inviting Fortune 500 companies to invest here. Since the Telangana state is a landlocked state, the CM said that he was consulting with Prime Minister Modi and the Chief Minister of the neighboring state, Chandrababu Naidu, to connect the Machilipatnam port via a 12-lane highway.

 We are striving to establish seamless connectivity through road, rail, port, and airport networks, as these will drive our growth. We are home to institutions like ISB, IIIT, and NALSAR University; we have focused on educational institutions and recognized the importance of human resources.  We are all discussing AI these days; AI is causing the loss of white-collar jobs. That is why we established the Young India Skills University—a public-private partnership. Anand Mahindra serves as the Chairman, and Srini Raju as the Vice-Chairman. We have transformed our ITIs into Advanced Technology Centres (ATCs) at a cost of ₹2,400 crore.  The Tata company is contributing 86 percent  and creating blue-collar jobs. I have  frequently visited Germany, Japan, and South Korea to study how blue-collar jobs are taking the place of white-collar jobs. Those in blue-collar roles earn more than IT engineers.  We are providing training in German, Japanese, and Korean languages to enable people to work in those countries. 

CENTRE’s INDIFFERENCE TOWARDS TELANGANA : 

The Chief minister criticized the union government for not extending financial assistance and also discriminated against  Telangana in approving investments.  In the past, short-term loans were secured at interest rates of 11 per cent  to 11.50 per cent. We are currently restructuring them with interest rates of 7 to 8 percent and converting them into long-term loans. We are in the process of restructuring debts worth ₹2 lakh crore. Neither the Centre nor the states are focusing on the flaws within the GST system. We have appointed Arvind Subramanian as a GST advisor. Over the past 7–8 years, monthly GST revenue never exceeded ₹3,500 crore, but for the last six months, it has crossed the ₹4,000 crore mark. We have generated an additional ₹5,000 crore in just six months. This was achieved by curbing corruption and plugging revenue leakages, without raising taxes.  We will fight against the Central Government's discrimination. Regarding investment approvals for our state, they are directing investors to go to Gujarat instead and this is the situation we are facing.

FARMERS – LOAN WAIVER :

 CM Revanth Reddy  highlighted the  measures taken for rescuing the distressed farmers for the last two years.   In the past, Telangana recorded the highest number of farmer suicides after Maharashtra, primarily due to debt. The Congress government waived loans amounting to ₹20,616 crore for 25,035 farming families which is the largest loan waiver in the country. An NCRB report—a report by the Central Government—stated that Telangana was a state with zero farmer suicides in the 2024-25 year. Farmers are happy. Previously, farmers had to struggle for the Minimum Support Price (MSP). Now,  we  ensured the MSP and also provided a bonus of ₹500 per quintal to paddy farmers. The Centre is neglecting crop procurement.  They simply announce the MRP and wash their hands of the matter. We are procuring Paddy and Maize, alongside others. Under the 'Rythu Bharosa' scheme, we provide ₹12,000 per acre, which farmers utilize for fertilizers and cultivation expenses.

WOMEN EMPOWERMENT : 

The Chief minister said that economic assistance is being provided to 6.7 million women in self-help groups across Telangana. They have availed loans worth ₹60,000 crore at zero interest, with the government bearing the interest costs. Women's groups have purchased 1,000 buses and also ventured into the renewable energy sector.  The government  has also allocated petrol bunks and solar plants to them. Members of these women's groups operate canteens at various government institutions, and we have entrusted them with the task of creating facilities in government schools.

REFORMS IN  EDUCATION :

 A slew of  measures were taken to strengthen the education in the  public sector,  the CM said that  we are introducing pre-schools. We have 27,000 government schools catering to 1.8 million (18 lakh) children, while there are 12,000 private schools with 3.5 million (35 lakh) children. Government teachers are highly qualified and many hold MA and PhD degrees. Yet, the children were not enrolling because  of lack of pre-school facilities.  We are also providing transport along with breakfast and mid-day meals to the students and sending the teachers to Singapore and other countries for study tours.

BUREAUCRACY :  

CM Revanth Reddy asserted that “ common sense is a crucial element of administration. If a problem is understood through common sense, half the  problem is solved and the rest is resolved through appropriate decision-making. If he  makes an opinion first, they tend to align their responses with it trying to please me. I spent 17 years in the opposition, from 2006 to 2023. During that time, I learned a great deal and fought for public causes. It was the reason no one can mislead me.

HYDRAA- LAKES  PROTECTION : 

The government's initiative  to protect the lakes and water bodies from the encroachments was discussed in the conversation. The Chief Minister said that  the government has established HYDRAA to remove all encroachments.  A senior IPS officer was appointed as the head of the  HYDRAA. Further, the CM said that    there are six major metropolitan cities: Delhi, Mumbai, Kolkata, Chennai, Hyderabad, and Bengaluru. Each of these cities should follow its own model to solve the encroachments, as well as strategies for environmental issues, water scarcity, and flash floods.

DRUG MENACE: 

Aiming to promote Telangana  as a drug free state , CM Revanth Reddy said that the 'Eagle Force' was set up to combat the drug menace, as students are falling victim to drugs. Our Eagle Force is the best in the country and our goal is to eradicate the drug problem completely.

CASTE CENSUS : 

The BC, SC, ST and minorities' welfare was given top priority in the government, the chief minister said that the main objective was to eliminate differences based on caste in education. The previous governments established separate residential schools for SCs, STs, BCs, and minorities. To truly eliminate casteism and foster unity without social barriers, we are now establishing 'Young India Integrated Schools' .   Following the Supreme Court's verdict, we also  implemented the categorization of SCs in our state. Even Gujarat has not implemented the Supreme Court's ruling . A caste census has not been conducted in the country since 1931. We conducted a caste census in our state; how can you extend welfare schemes to Backward Classes (BCs) without a caste census?

To a question,  the CM clarified that he does not resort to abuse and speaks sarcastically. He never argued with journalists and threatened any one for writing against him. He viewed the media as a source of 'back-office' information. He also regularly holds press conferences every ten days and answers every question asked. The CM emphasized that true understanding comes only from connecting with the people. Connecting with the public is the real strength in public life.

POLITICAL JOURNEY :

CM Revanth Reddy narrated how he grew in politics as a leader of the student wing (Vidyarthi Parishad),  ventured into business and later elected as an  independent ZPTC member and MLC in  2007. Subsequently, he  joined the TDP and worked under the leadership of Chandrababu Naidu for ten years. He  was elected as an MLA twice. Due to the state bifurcation and local factors, he resigned from the TDP.  At that time, he  had several options before him but decided to join the Congress party because it was the Congress that granted statehood to Telangana.  Sonia Gandhi fulfilled the 60-year-old dream of the people of Telangana. When he  joined the party, he  apprised Rahul Gandhi of every detail regarding my political journey. He  became the PCC President and the Chief Minister. By July 2026, he will have completed 20 years in public life. Throughout his  political career, he has fought for the people and the common man. He came from an agricultural family and his father was a Police Patel. Without any political background or backing,  ours is a family defined by a strong work ethic. He reached this position thanks to the blessings of the people of Telangana.
@the_hindu

text:
Meta must stop silently withholding the Instagram accounts of independent journalists in India

13 October 2026

Since 9 October 2026, Instagram has made the accounts of several independent journalists covering the protests in Delhi unavailable in India. Utkarsh Gaur’s main account was withheld on 9 October, and Sunny Tomar’s soon after. On the night of 12 October, Instagram withheld the account of Shubhangi Das Gupta, a 22-year-old independent journalist, and her secondary account now appears to face the same action. Today, Journo Mirror’s account was withheld in India. Each received the same notice, that Instagram had, “temporarily restricted access to this account pursuant to legal requirements under India’s Information Technology (Intermediary Guidelines and Digital Media Ethics Code) Rules.” The notice does not say which authority made the demand, which rule was invoked, which post was objected to, or when the “temporary” restriction ends. It arrives as a no-reply notification after the account has gone dark, with no prior warning and no reason.

The same day, IANS and ANI, citing Delhi Police sources, reported that around 500 posts “spreading rumours or trying to create unrest among people” had been taken down. On 12 October, PTI had put the figure at 300, which means about 200 more in one day. The police have not said which posts were removed, from which platforms, under which provision, or whether anyone who posted them was told. We are also receiving reports of WhatsApp accounts being shut down and of mobile numbers being put through fresh KYC verification that leaves them unusable while it is pending. All of this comes alongside a timeline in which there was suspension of internet services and public transport in the heart of the national capital.

IFF condemns Meta’s withholding of entire journalist accounts on the strength of an unnamed “legal requirement”, and the Delhi Police’s practice of announcing a running censorship tally through anonymous sources. Meta must restore these accounts, tell every affected user who asked for the restriction and under what law, and stop turning demands about particular posts into the silencing of entire accounts.
The IT Rules, 2021, on which Meta’s notice relies, give it two routes to restrict content. The notice meets the conditions of neither. If Meta acted on a government demand, the route is Rule 3(1)(d). If Meta acted on its own, Rule 4(8) requires it, as a significant social media intermediary, to notify the user before disabling access, explain the grounds, and give an adequate opportunity to dispute the action. None of this happened. In this situation at present the entire burden will be shifted to the user to seek remedy under Rules 3(2) and 3A, where a user must first go to Meta’s Grievance Officer, who has 15 days, and then to the Grievance Appellate Committee, which has 30 more. In our experience these timelines are often not met, and a grievance against unnamed “legal requirements” is likely to be answered by pointing back to them. Whatever the intention, the effect is to keep a journalist off the platform for more than six weeks, exactly when her reporting matters most.

The Delhi Police figures raise their own questions. “Rumour” is not a ground for restricting speech under Article 19(2).  A count of 500 posts announced through unnamed sources does not let anyone tell whether a post was fabricated or simply showed something the police did not want seen. Nor is it obvious that 200 reasoned intimations, each signed by an officer of DIG rank and each identifying the provision, the unlawful act and the exact URL, were issued in a single day.

Our demands

1) Meta should restore every account withheld in connection with the protests where the underlying demand, if any, concerned specific posts, and restrict no more than the URLs named in a lawful reasoned intimation.
2) Meta should tell each affected user in writing which authority made the demand, the issuing officer’s rank, the provision relied on, the content identified, and when the restriction will end.
3) Meta should disclose whether its systems automatically extend demands about individual posts to entire accounts, and stop any such escalation immediately.
4) The Delhi Police should publish the takedown requests it has issued, with their number, platforms, provisions, issuing officers and reasons, as Anuradha Bhasin requires.
5) MeitY should ensure notice and a hearing to every person whose content is restricted, publish the outcome of the monthly Secretary-level review under Rule 3(1)(d), and stop using Section 79(3)(b), the Sahyog Portal and “temporary” restrictions under the IT Rules to bypass the safeguards of Section 69A.
If you have been affected

If your post or account was withheld or removed in connection with the protests, or you received a notice about a police data request, write to legal@internetfreedom.in for pro bono assistance. Keep screenshots of every notice, note the date and time, and delete nothing. Document, document, document.

text:
My wife emptied our joint account, moved her 25-year-old boyfriend into my house, and sent me a kiss emoji after leaving me with two cents. 

She thought being thousands of miles away meant I couldn’t stop her. 

She forgot one thing: my cousin had already seen the message where her boyfriend discussed my death.

It was 3:00 a.m. on an oil rig in the Persian Gulf when Christa’s message came through.

I’d just finished a fourteen-hour shift. 

My back hurt, my hands smelled of grease and saltwater, and all I wanted was a shower and a few hours of sleep.

Instead, I opened a text that changed everything.

I’m leaving you, Miles. 

Devon and I are moving to Palm Springs. 

I’m taking what’s mine. Enjoy being alone.

A second message followed.

It was a screenshot of our joint bank account.

Balance: $0.02.

Then she sent a kiss emoji.

I stared at the screen, waiting for the anger to hit me. 

It didn’t come right away. At first, I felt embarrassed. 

I’d spent fifteen years working overseas, missing birthdays, holidays, and ordinary evenings at home because I believed I was building a secure future for my wife and me.

Apparently, I’d been building one for her and somebody else.

I could have called her. I could have sent a dozen furious messages.

Instead, I typed, Good luck, Christa.

Then I put my phone away.

She probably expected me to spend the night begging her to reconsider. 

She’d always believed I couldn’t stand the thought of losing her.

What she didn’t know was that my cousin Brendan had been looking into our finances for weeks.

And he’d found something far worse than a missing $142,000.

The following morning, I checked my email and found divorce papers. 

Christa claimed I’d abandoned our marriage by working overseas. 

Her lawyer was already seeking spousal support based on my income.

She’d also described Devon as her partner and claimed he was living in our house.

The house in Odessa.

The one I’d spent fifteen years paying for.

I forwarded everything to Brendan, a forensic accountant in Houston.

Activate Protocol Winter, I wrote.

Brendan and I had come up with that plan years earlier after a friend from the oil industry returned home to discover that his accounts had been drained and his financial records had mysteriously disappeared. 

We promised each other we’d never be caught completely unprepared.

Protocol Winter was simple: preserve everything before anyone could erase it.

Bank statements. 

Property documents. 

Emails. 

Insurance records. 

Account histories.

Anything that might matter later.

Brendan replied within minutes.

Already started. 

Don’t contact her. 

Let me finish checking the records.

So I went back to work.

For the next two weeks, Christa tried everything she could to get a reaction out of me.

She sent a picture of Devon drinking from my father’s old whiskey glasses.

Then she sent another showing him sitting behind my grandfather’s restored desk, his muddy boots resting on the wood.

Maybe if you’d spent more time at home, I wouldn’t have needed someone else, she wrote.

I read the message, locked my phone, and returned to my shift.

text:
It wasn’t easy. 

I was furious. 

But Brendan kept reminding me that every angry message I sent could become something her lawyer used against me.

Meanwhile, he was finding things I couldn’t explain away.

The $142,000 hadn’t disappeared in one transaction. 

It had been moved through several transfers over fourteen months, including payments into an account Christa had never told me about.

There was also a $40,000 home-equity line opened against the house. 

The signature on the paperwork looked similar to mine, but I hadn’t applied for the loan.

Then Brendan found a change to my life-insurance beneficiary.

That change had been filed while I was working offshore.

I asked him to send everything to my attorney.

He told me he already had.

Then, one morning, he called me through an encrypted app. 

His voice sounded different from usual.

Miles, I’ve found a backup of a conversation between Christa and Devon. I need you to listen carefully.

I sat down.

He read the message aloud.

Plan B. It’s just insurance money. 

He works a dangerous job for a reason. 

Accidents happen all the time.

For a few seconds, I couldn’t speak.

I could hear the rig’s machinery through the wall and the steady rush of wind outside. 

Somewhere below me, black seawater moved around the steel legs of the platform.

I’d spent years working in dangerous places. 

I’d accepted the risks because I thought the people waiting for me at home were worth it.

Now I was reading a message suggesting that someone at home might be counting on those risks to solve a problem.

Have you sent that to the lawyer? I finally asked.

Yes. He’s preserving the original files and working with the authorities. Don’t confront either of them.

I looked down at my hands.

Brendan, I need to get home.

I know. 

But we’re going to do this properly.

By the time I landed in Texas, my attorney had filed the necessary requests to protect the house and challenge the suspicious financial transactions. 

The bank had also flagged the disputed home-equity loan and begun reviewing the transfers.

Christa’s story was beginning to fall apart.

She’d filed a domestic-violence petition claiming I’d threatened her in person on dates when my offshore work records placed me thousands of miles away. 

My attorney had my travel documents, work logs, and other records ready for the court.

Suddenly, my phone wouldn’t stop ringing.

Please call me, Miles.

Something terrible is happening.

Devon says the bank has frozen the money. 

What did you do?

I didn’t answer.

I wanted the facts established before another conversation turned into an argument about who had hurt whom.

Instead, I drove straight to Odessa.

Before sunrise, I parked at my neighbor Harold’s house across the street from my property. 

He’d known my family for years and had been keeping an eye on the place.

At 8:20 that morning, a rental truck pulled into my driveway.

Christa came out carrying a clipboard. 

Devon followed her, directing two hired movers as they loaded my belongings.

Not her clothes. 

Not the furniture she’d bought.

My grandfather’s desk.

My father’s watch collection.

text:
The silver picture frames my grandmother had kept on her mantel for decades.

Devon dragged the desk across the porch, scraping one of its legs against the wood.

Harold stood beside me, watching in disbelief.

That’s your grandfather’s desk, isn’t it?

Yes.

Want me to call the police?

I checked the time.

No need. 

My attorney arranged for the court officer to meet us here.

At 8:55, a sedan pulled in behind the rental truck.

Two deputies stepped out, followed by a court officer carrying a thick folder.

Christa opened the front door with an irritated expression, clearly expecting another delivery.

Then she saw the badges.

Her face changed.

Devon walked up behind her, trying to look confident.

What’s going on? he demanded. 

We’re just moving our belongings.

The court officer asked them to step onto the porch.

That’s when I crossed the street.

Christa saw me coming and went completely still.

Miles? What are you doing here?

I stopped at the bottom of the steps.

I live here.

You were supposed to be on the rig.

I came home.

She looked past me, as if expecting someone to explain how I’d managed to appear in my own driveway.

Devon recovered first.

This is a private matter between a husband and wife, he said. 

You can’t just show up and interfere.

One of the deputies asked him to step back.

The court officer opened the folder.

Mr. Cross, Ms. 

Christa Whitaker, this order prohibits the removal or disposal of the listed property while the ownership dispute is being reviewed. 

The disputed financial transactions and the loan application are also subject to investigation.

Christa began speaking immediately.

Those are our savings. 

I’m entitled to half. 

Miles has been gone for years. 

I was left to manage everything.

The court officer didn’t argue with her.

That is a matter for the court to determine. 

It does not authorize you to transfer disputed funds or remove property covered by this order.

Devon glanced at the truck.

Then he looked toward the street.

The court officer turned another page.

There’s also a request for preservation of electronic evidence related to the life-insurance beneficiary change and messages that may be relevant to an investigation into possible financial fraud and a suspected plan to cause harm.

Christa’s mouth fell open.

Devon stopped moving.

I watched his confidence disappear as the officer explained that the messages had been preserved and referred to the appropriate authorities. 

No one was declaring either of them guilty on the porch, but the matter was no longer something they could settle by deleting a conversation or telling a different story.

Then the officer handed Devon a document.

His eyes moved across the page.

What is this? he asked.

An instruction requiring you to preserve relevant records and comply with the investigation. 

You should speak to your attorney before answering questions.

Devon looked at Christa.

She stared back at him.

For the first time since I’d arrived, neither of them had anything to say.

And I finally understood why.

I have my twitter back. 

It took me 6 days, a cyber police complaint and a legal notice to twitter to recover my account. 

If you got a DM from me last week asking you to vote for me for a podcast, that was not me. Please don't click it & If you already did, please change your password ASAP.

Here's what happened:

→I received a late night DM from a friend to vote on a podcast which redirected me to a a login page that looked right, and I typed in my password (classic)

→The attacker logged in and changed my 2FA within minutes & I was locked out of my account. (I still don't understand how my email and phone number were changed. Neither my email nor my phone was compromised.)

→Then he used account to DM followers a fake "vote for me" link. Each person who clicks becomes the next account sending it. That is how these spread.

What didn't work:

→ I filed X's hacked account form within the hour. Less than two hours later, the reply came: X could not verify me as the account owner. Their suggestion was to create a new account. Once 2FA is changed, the automated system treats the attacker as the real owner.

→ So I went to the Grievance Officer. Under the IT Rules, 2021, X must appoint a Resident Grievance Officer in India. He has no email address. X does not accept legal notices by email. 

The only options are a web form or post to their physical office.

Here's what worked:

→First, a cyber complaint on https://t.co/Uzds8BObDW (or call 1930).

→Second, a legal notice to the Grievance Officer. Under the IT Rules, impersonation complaints must be acted on within 24 hours.

→Third, the same notice sent by registered post, and to every X email address I could find.

The notice put X on record. It set out the ticket number, the phishing link, and the cyber complaint number. It showed proof of ownership: the registered email, the phone number, and the Premium subscription paid from my card. It ended with a clear ask and a deadline.

Six days after the hack, I was back in.

If this happens to you:
• Act within hours
• File X's hacked account form from your registered email and be persistent (this is important)
• File at https://t.co/Uzds8BObDW and keep the acknowledgement
• Notice to the Grievance Officer via the https://t.co/YkDfcMQwzE form and by post

Hence I argue - that Right To Time - should be a fundamental right! The right to be heard in time.

Maybe the judges are busy, they are legal experts, not Managment experts. Why does CJI remain master of roster and why is there no separate CEO and separate process for determining which matter will be heard when? 

If Delhi HC or SC had heard the matter yesterday, could all that is happening today be avoided?

Why is everything in the legal system - in the aftermath?! 

When lawyers are no more safe, when citizens are not safe, when journalists are not safe - we should deeply be worried about the state of our legal system then blindly succumbing to it.

Also notice how ‘obedience’ has been so ingrained in our citizens for all higher up authorities - the young of this country are challenging that. 

I hope my party and my leader @RahulGandhi will start a nation wide movement for legal reforms in India.

Satyameva Jayate!
Today justice does not seem to be done even if there are takers to argue that it is being done!

Hello everyone,

My name is Mohammad Wasim, and I am a former employee of AU Small Finance Bank.

On September 21, I experienced an online fraud while attempting to make a purchase worth ₹399 through the DMart app. I did not receive any purchase confirmation, but at around 1:26 AM, I started receiving OTPs automatically from nyka . I did not share any OTP with anyone, yet fraudulent transactions took place from my two bank credit card accounts.

The following amounts were fraudulently debited from my accounts:

- AU Bank: ₹99,989
- ICICI Bank: ₹78,000 and ₹45,508

It is extremely unfair that, despite reporting the incident promptly and cooperating with the authorities, I am being asked to repay money that was fraudulently taken from my account.

I urgently need guidance on how to recover my money and protect my CIBIL score from being affected by these disputed transactions.

I sincerely request everyone to guide me on where I can escalate this matter and what steps I should take to recover my hard-earned money.

Your support and suggestions would mean a lot to me during this difficult time.

Thank you for your understanding and support. 🙏
Mohd Wasim
